SPECIAL TESTS__Endocrine — Adrenal & Pit:
The Short Synacthen Test (SST), also called the short ACTH stimulation or tetracosactide test, is a dynamic assessment of the adrenal cortex’s capacity to secrete cortisol. It is the standard first-line investigation used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency — whether primary (Addison’s disease) or long-standing secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) disease in which the adrenal has atrophied.

1Indication & principle

Requested when adrenal insufficiency is suspected: unexplained fatigue, weight loss, hypotension/postural drop, hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hyperpigmentation, or a low/borderline morning (9 am) cortisol. The synthetic ACTH analogue tetracosactide (Synacthen) reproduces the biological action of endogenous ACTH, binding melanocortin-2 receptors on the adrenal cortex to drive cortisol synthesis.

A healthy adrenal responds briskly with a cortisol surge.
A diseased or atrophied adrenal cannot mount an adequate rise — the response is blunted or absent.
It tests the adrenal gland’s reserve, not the pituitary’s ability to secrete ACTH.
2How it is performed

Best done in the morning. The patient need not be fasted, but omit any hydrocortisone dose beforehand as it cross-reacts in the cortisol assay (prednisolone/dexamethasone can be substituted if steroid cover is essential).

Take a baseline (0 min) serum cortisol (some centres add baseline ACTH & renin).
Give 250 µg tetracosactide IM or IV (standard-dose SST).
Repeat serum cortisol at 30 min, and often 60 min.
Interpretation rests on the PEAK stimulated cortisol, not the increment alone.
3Interpretation & cut-offs

Thresholds are assay-dependent — the classic polyclonal cut-off is >550 nmol/L, but modern monoclonal immunoassays and LC-MS/MS use lower targets (~>420–450 nmol/L). Always read against the local laboratory’s reference.

Peak cortisol >550 nmol/L (classic assay)→Normal adrenal reserve — primary adrenal insufficiency excluded
Peak cortisol ~>420–450 nmol/L (newer monoclonal/LC-MS assay)→Adequate response per that assay’s threshold
Subnormal / failed rise below threshold→Adrenal insufficiency confirmed — start lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone), adding fludrocortisone if primary (Addison's)
Failed rise + HIGH paired ACTH→Primary (Addison’s disease)
Failed rise + LOW / inappropriately normal ACTH→Secondary (pituitary/hypothalamic) with adrenal atrophy
4Pitfalls & limitations

The SST’s key blind spot is recent-onset secondary insufficiency: after acute pituitary damage or abrupt steroid withdrawal the adrenal has not yet atrophied, so it still responds to exogenous ACTH and the SST can be falsely normal. Here the insulin tolerance test (ITT) — which probes the whole HPA axis — is the gold standard.

🧪Baseline cortisol
Starting point at 0 min
💉Tetracosactide
250 µg synthetic ACTH stimulus
⏱️Peak cortisol
Measured at 30 ± 60 min
🧭Paired ACTH
Distinguishes primary vs secondary
🚩 Never delay hydrocortisone to complete the test in a patient with suspected adrenal crisis — treat empirically (IV hydrocortisone + fluids) and confirm the diagnosis later. Dexamethasone does not cross-react in the cortisol assay, so it can cover the patient during testing.
🎓 A 9 am cortisol <100 nmol/L makes adrenal insufficiency very likely and >450–500 nmol/L makes it unlikely; intermediate values are exactly where the SST earns its place. Remember: recent oral oestrogen / combined pill raises cortisol-binding globulin and can spuriously elevate total cortisol — ideally stop it ~6 weeks before testing.

The 9am serum cortisol and the overnight 1mg dexamethasone suppression test (ODST) are the two everyday screening tests of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, sitting at opposite ends of the spectrum. A basal 9am cortisol screens for adrenal insufficiency (too little cortisol), while the ODST screens for Cushing’s syndrome (too much cortisol). Both exploit the normal diurnal rhythm of cortisol, and both are simple, cheap first-line filters that flag who needs definitive dynamic or confirmatory testing.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Cortisol secretion follows a diurnal rhythm: highest around 8–9am (the peak) and lowest around midnight (the nadir). The two tests use this in opposite directions.

9am cortisol — requested when adrenal insufficiency is suspected (fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperpigmentation, or after long-term/withdrawn glucocorticoids). It samples at the physiological peak, when a healthy axis should easily generate a high level.
Overnight 1mg ODST — requested when cortisol excess is suspected (central obesity, striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, hypertension, new/resistant diabetes). Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic steroid that suppresses ACTH via negative feedback but is not detected by the cortisol assay; a normal axis therefore switches off endogenous cortisol.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
🕘9am cortisol
Single serum sample drawn between 08:00 and 09:00; patient need not be fasting. Avoid during acute stress if possible.
💊Dexamethasone dose
1mg dexamethasone taken orally at 23:00 (bedtime).
🩸Morning sample
Serum cortisol measured at 09:00 the following morning (~10h after the dose).
📋Preparation
Confirm compliance and timing; review interfering drugs (enzyme inducers) and oestrogen-containing preparations before booking.
3INTERPRETATION — THE CUT-OFFS

9am cortisol (screening for adrenal insufficiency):

9am cortisol <100 nmol/L→Adrenal insufficiency likely — proceed to Short Synacthen Test (and treat if unwell)
9am cortisol 100–400 nmol/L→Indeterminate — cannot exclude insufficiency; dynamic testing (Synacthen) required
9am cortisol >400–500 nmol/L→Intact axis — adrenal insufficiency very unlikely

Overnight 1mg ODST (screening for Cushing’s syndrome):

Post-dexamethasone cortisol <50 nmol/L→Normal suppression — Cushing’s syndrome excluded (negative screen)
Post-dexamethasone cortisol >50 nmol/L→Failure to suppress — positive screen; refer for confirmatory work-up (48h low-dose test, late-night salivary cortisol, 24h urinary free cortisol)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Assay measures total cortisol. Oestrogens (combined pill, pregnancy, HRT) raise cortisol-binding globulin (CBG), inflating total cortisol and causing false-positive non-suppression on the ODST.
Accelerated dexamethasone metabolism. Enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin) clear dexamethasone faster, so suppression fails despite a normal axis.
Pseudo-Cushing’s states. Severe depression, chronic alcohol excess, acute illness and obesity can activate the HPA axis and blunt suppression, mimicking true Cushing’s.
Timing errors. A 9am cortisol drawn late loses the diurnal advantage; poor compliance with the 23:00 dexamethasone dose invalidates the ODST.
🚩 A single 9am cortisol should NEVER be used to withhold steroids in a patient who is acutely unwell or shocked. If adrenal crisis is suspected, take the cortisol (and ACTH) sample but give hydrocortisone immediately — do not wait for the result. During major physiological stress cortisol should be high, so a “normal” or low value in a critically ill patient is inappropriate and points to insufficiency.
🎓 Remember the direction of the diurnal clock: sample cortisol at its 9am peak to catch a deficiency (it should be high then), and give dexamethasone at its midnight nadir to catch an excess (it should be off then). Dexamethasone is chosen precisely because it suppresses ACTH yet is invisible to the cortisol immunoassay, so any measured cortisol is purely endogenous.

The dexamethasone suppression tests are dynamic endocrine tests that exploit negative feedback on the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. Dexamethasone is a potent synthetic glucocorticoid that suppresses pituitary ACTH (and hence cortisol) in a normal axis but does not cross-react in the cortisol assay. The low-dose test (LDDST) CONFIRMS whether pathological cortisol excess (Cushing’s syndrome) is present after a positive screen; the high-dose test (HDDST) helps LOCALISE the cause once excess is proven, and is always interpreted alongside a plasma ACTH.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to work up suspected Cushing’s syndrome (central obesity, proximal myopathy, striae, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, easy bruising) once a screening test is positive. Screening options include late-night salivary cortisol, 24h urinary free cortisol, or the overnight 1mg dexamethasone test.

Physiological logic: in a healthy axis, exogenous glucocorticoid feedback switches off ACTH, so morning cortisol falls (“suppresses”).
Autonomous cortisol production (adrenal tumour) or an ACTH source resistant to normal feedback (ectopic ACTH) fails to suppress.
A pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing’s disease) retains partial feedback sensitivity — it resists low doses but is suppressed by high doses.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Low-dose (LDDST): 0.5 mg oral dexamethasone every 6 hours for 48 hours; measure serum cortisol at 0h and at 48h (6h after the last dose). The overnight 1 mg variant (1 mg at 23:00, cortisol at 08:00–09:00) is a simpler outpatient alternative used mainly for screening.

High-dose (HDDST): 2 mg oral dexamethasone every 6 hours for 48 hours (or an overnight 8 mg version), with cortisol measured before and after. Take a paired plasma ACTH to classify the axis. Ensure the patient is not on interfering drugs and that pseudo-Cushing’s states have been considered before interpreting.

🧪LDDST
0.5mg q6h × 48h — confirms Cushing’s syndrome
🧪HDDST
2mg q6h × 48h — localises the cause
🩸Plasma ACTH
splits ACTH-dependent vs ACTH-independent
🧭BIPSS / CRH
pituitary vs ectopic ACTH source
3INTERPRETATION

LDDST — does the patient HAVE Cushing’s?

Cortisol suppresses to <50 nmol/L→Normal axis — Cushing’s syndrome excluded
Cortisol FAILS to suppress (≥50 nmol/L)→Confirms Cushing’s syndrome (pathological cortisol excess)

ACTH — which arm of the axis?

ACTH low / suppressed→ACTH-independent — adrenal cause (adenoma / carcinoma)
ACTH normal / high→ACTH-dependent — pituitary disease or ectopic ACTH

HDDST — WHERE is the source?

Cortisol suppresses by ≥50%→Pituitary Cushing’s DISEASE (feedback partly retained)
No suppression, ACTH high→Ectopic ACTH (e.g. small-cell lung, carcinoid)
No suppression, ACTH low→Adrenal tumour (autonomous cortisol)

To finally separate pituitary from ectopic ACTH, bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is the gold standard: a central (petrosal) : peripheral ACTH gradient localises the source to the pituitary. The CRH stimulation test complements this — pituitary adenomas respond to CRH with an exaggerated ACTH/cortisol rise, whereas ectopic sources typically do not.

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Pseudo-Cushing’s: chronic alcohol excess, severe depression, obesity and poorly controlled diabetes can activate the HPA axis and cause failure to suppress — a false positive.
Drug interference: enzyme inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin) accelerate dexamethasone metabolism → falsely non-suppressed result.
Oestrogens / pregnancy raise cortisol-binding globulin and total cortisol, distorting the assay; the combined oral contraceptive should ideally be stopped ~6 weeks before testing.
HDDST is imperfect: up to ~10% of ectopic tumours suppress and some pituitary adenomas do not, so it never replaces BIPSS for definitive localisation.
🚩 A “failure to suppress” is not automatically Cushing’s — exclude pseudo-Cushing’s and drug/oestrogen interference before committing a patient to imaging or surgery. Never interpret the cortisol result without the paired ACTH and the drug history.
🎓 One-line examiner mnemonic: LOW dose = “Do they HAVE it?”; HIGH dose = “WHERE is it?”. Pituitary disease suppresses on high dose (partial feedback retained); ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours do NOT.

The Insulin Tolerance Test (ITT), also called the insulin stress test, is the historical gold-standard dynamic test of the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the growth hormone (GH) axis. A weight-based dose of soluble insulin is given IV to induce controlled hypoglycaemia — a potent physiological stressor that, in a healthy pituitary, provokes a brisk rise in both GH and cortisol (the latter driven by ACTH). Blunted responses point to GH deficiency and/or secondary (ACTH-dependent) adrenal insufficiency.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to assess ACTH and GH reserve, typically after pituitary surgery, in suspected hypopituitarism, and where GH deficiency in adults must be confirmed before replacement. Hypoglycaemia is sensed by the hypothalamus as a life-threatening stress, activating the counter-regulatory response.

Physiological logic: a real, adequate hypoglycaemic stimulus (glucose <2.2 mmol/L) is required to validly stress both axes simultaneously.
Key advantage: the ITT detects recent-onset secondary adrenal insufficiency that the Short Synacthen Test can miss, because the adrenal glands have not yet atrophied.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed fasted, in the morning, with an indwelling IV cannula and continuous close medical supervision. IV 50% dextrose and hydrocortisone must be drawn up and immediately available.

Dose: soluble insulin 0.15 U/kg IV (0.1 U/kg if hypopituitarism likely; up to 0.3 U/kg in insulin-resistant states, e.g. Cushing's/acromegaly).
Sampling: measure glucose, cortisol and GH at 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 and 120 minutes.
Endpoint of stimulus: the test is only valid once adequate hypoglycaemia with symptoms (sweating, tachycardia) is achieved.
3INTERPRETATION

A valid test requires demonstrable hypoglycaemia; the peak hormone values are then read against established cut-offs (assay-dependent).

Glucose <2.2 mmol/L with symptoms→adequate stimulus — test is valid to interpret
Peak cortisol ≥500 nmol/L→intact HPA axis — ACTH/cortisol reserve excluded
Peak cortisol <500 nmol/L→inadequate response — secondary adrenal insufficiency
Peak GH ≥5–7 µg/L→normal somatotroph reserve — GH deficiency excluded
Peak GH <3 µg/L→severe adult GH deficiency — supports GH replacement
Suspected GH EXCESS (acromegaly)→the ITT tests GH deficiency; for GH excess use IGF-1 + the OGTT GH-suppression test (GH fails to fall <0.4 µg/L = positive) → pituitary MRI. Acromegaly ›
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
🧪Inadequate hypoglycaemia
if glucose never falls <2.2 mmol/L the test is uninterpretable and must be repeated with a higher dose
💉Over-treatment
giving IV dextrose too early aborts the stimulus and invalidates results — treat only for severe/neuroglycopenic symptoms
📉Assay dependence
cortisol cut-offs vary with the immunoassay used; modern assays may use lower thresholds than the classic 500 nmol/L
🕒Supervision burden
labour-intensive and potentially dangerous, so alternatives (glucagon test, Synacthen) are used when the ITT is unsafe
🚩 CRITICAL: The ITT is CONTRAINDICATED in ischaemic heart disease (obtain a baseline ECG), epilepsy/seizure disorders, and untreated hypothyroidism or established adrenal insufficiency. It must only be done under close medical supervision with a doctor present and IV dextrose and hydrocortisone ready to treat severe hypoglycaemia, which can cause seizures, arrhythmia or death.
🎓 Exam pearl: The ITT stresses two axes at once — a single valid test gives both GH and ACTH/cortisol reserve. Remember its unique edge: it can unmask early secondary adrenal insufficiency (e.g. weeks after pituitary surgery) when the adrenals still respond to exogenous Synacthen and the SST is falsely normal.

The 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) and late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) are two of the three first-line screening tests for Cushing’s syndrome (the third being the overnight/low-dose dexamethasone suppression test). Rather than measuring a single random cortisol — which is uninterpretable because of the steep circadian rhythm and stress-driven pulsatility — each of these tests captures a physiological signature of pathological cortisol excess: the UFC integrates total free cortisol thrown into the urine across a whole day, while the LNSC exploits loss of the normal midnight nadir. They screen for the presence of hypercortisolism; they do NOT localise the cause.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used when Cushing’s syndrome is clinically suspected: proximal myopathy, thin skin with easy bruising, wide purple striae, central obesity, moon facies, new hypertension or diabetes, osteoporosis, or psychiatric change. The two tests probe different facets of the same disease:

24h UFC — normally ∼90% of circulating cortisol is protein-bound (to cortisol-binding globulin); only the small free fraction is filtered into urine. In cortisol excess, binding globulin saturates, so free cortisol — and hence urinary excretion — rises disproportionately. It gives an integrated measure of daily secretion, smoothing out pulsatility.
Late-night salivary cortisol — salivary cortisol reflects the free, biologically active fraction and tracks plasma cortisol closely. Healthy people reach their cortisol nadir around midnight; in Cushing’s this trough is lost, so a raised midnight value is an early, sensitive marker.
🎓 The unifying concept across BOTH tests is loss of the circadian rhythm combined with saturation of cortisol-binding globulin. Grasp that one idea and you can reason out why an integrated 24h collection AND a single well-timed midnight sample each expose the same underlying autonomous hypercortisolism.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
24h UFC: the patient discards the first morning void, then collects every subsequent void for 24 hours including the next morning’s first void, into a container. A simultaneous urinary creatinine confirms the collection is complete and adequate. Because output is variable, 2–3 separate collections are recommended before acting on the result.
Late-night salivary cortisol: a convenient outpatient/home test. The patient chews or holds a cotton swab (Salivette) at home between 23:00 and midnight, avoiding eating, drinking, brushing teeth or smoking beforehand. Usually collected on two separate nights. No venepuncture and no admission needed — well suited to children and to avoiding the stress artefact of a needle.
3INTERPRETATION

Results are read against the local assay’s reference range — always use lab-specific cut-offs — but the following patterns are what examiners expect:

24h UFC within normal range on repeated collections→Cushing’s syndrome effectively excluded (high negative predictive value)
24h UFC mildly raised (up to ∼3× upper limit of normal)→Suggestive but non-specific — overlaps with pseudo-Cushing’s; repeat and corroborate with a second test
24h UFC markedly raised (>3–4× upper limit of normal)→Highly suggestive of genuine cortisol excess
Late-night salivary cortisol elevated (above assay cut-off)→Loss of circadian nadir — sensitive positive screen for Cushing’s
Late-night salivary cortisol normal (rhythm preserved)→Cushing’s unlikely — strong argument against active hypercortisolism
TWO different first-line tests clearly abnormal→Hypercortisolism confirmed → proceed to establish the cause (measure ACTH etc.)
🧪24h UFC
Integrated daily free-cortisol excretion; repeat 2–3×
🌙Late-night salivary
Detects lost midnight nadir; convenient home test
💊Overnight DST
Third first-line test; failure to suppress = positive
🎯Confirm rule
Need ≥2 different tests abnormal before diagnosis
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

No single screening test is perfectly specific, so both are prone to false positives and false negatives:

24h UFC pitfalls: incomplete collection gives a falsely LOW result; very high fluid intake can spuriously raise it; day-to-day variability and mild elevations overlap with pseudo-Cushing’s. It can be falsely reassuring in mild/cyclical disease.
Salivary cortisol pitfalls: shift work or an erratic sleep–wake cycle abolishes the normal rhythm and mimics disease; acute illness, contamination of the swab (e.g. topical/oral steroid, blood from gums, food, licorice) and smoking all distort the result.
Pseudo-Cushing’s: depression, chronic alcohol excess, severe obesity, poorly controlled diabetes and physiological stress can all mildly raise cortisol and its urinary/salivary markers — the great mimic to keep in mind before labelling a patient.
🚩 A single mildly abnormal test does NOT diagnose Cushing’s — and a single normal one does not fully exclude it in cyclical disease. Shift workers, the acutely unwell, and patients with depression or alcohol excess (pseudo-Cushing’s) generate false positives; contamination invalidates salivary samples. Always require at least TWO different first-line tests to be abnormal, repeat before acting, and interpret against the local assay’s reference range.

The aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR) is the screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) — autonomous aldosterone secretion from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. It is a leading treatable cause of secondary/resistant hypertension, classically with hypokalaemia (though potassium is often normal). A positive ARR is followed by a confirmatory suppression test (usually the saline suppression test), then adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling to decide surgery versus medical therapy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

In health, aldosterone is driven by the renin–angiotensin system: low renal perfusion → renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone. In primary hyperaldosteronism, the adrenal secretes aldosterone autonomously, so the resulting sodium retention and volume expansion suppress renin. The hallmark is therefore HIGH aldosterone with LOW/suppressed renin → a raised ARR.

Screen: resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on ≥3 drugs), hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalaemia.
Screen: hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma, or with a family history of early hypertension/stroke.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — ARR SCREEN & PREPARATION

A paired morning (mid-morning, seated/ambulant) sample measures plasma aldosterone and plasma renin (renin activity or direct renin concentration). Correct preparation is essential to avoid false results.

Correct hypokalaemia first — low potassium suppresses aldosterone and can mask the diagnosis.
Ensure liberal (not restricted) sodium intake and stop drugs that distort the ratio.
🚫MR antagonists
Spironolactone / eplerenone stopped ~4–6 weeks before — they invalidate the test
💊ACEi / ARB
Raise renin → can lower ARR (false negative)
💊Beta-blockers
Suppress renin → raise ARR (false positive)
✅Safe switches
Doxazosin (α-blocker) & verapamil have least effect on the ratio
3INTERPRETATION & CONFIRMATION

A raised ARR is a screening flag, not a diagnosis — it must be confirmed. The saline suppression test exploits normal physiology: an IV saline load expands volume and should suppress aldosterone. In primary hyperaldosteronism aldosterone stays inappropriately high (fails to suppress).

↑ Aldosterone + suppressed renin → raised ARR→Positive screen — proceed to confirmatory testing
Saline suppression: post-infusion aldosterone remains HIGH (fails to suppress)→Confirms primary hyperaldosteronism
Saline suppression: aldosterone falls / suppresses appropriately→Primary hyperaldosteronism excluded
HIGH aldosterone WITH high renin→Secondary hyperaldosteronism (e.g. renal artery stenosis, diuretics) — NOT Conn's

Alternatives to IV saline are the fludrocortisone suppression test or oral salt loading. Once confirmed: adrenal CT then adrenal vein sampling to lateralise.

🎯Unilateral adenoma
Lateralised on vein sampling → laparoscopic adrenalectomy
⚖️Bilateral hyperplasia
No lateralisation → lifelong MR antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Uncorrected hypokalaemia and interfering drugs are the commonest causes of false results.
Adrenal CT alone can mislead — a non-functioning incidentaloma may be present, or a dominant nodule may be the non-secreting side; vein sampling is the reference standard for lateralisation.
Renin at the very low end can produce a spuriously high ratio, so a minimum aldosterone level is usually required alongside the ratio.
🚩 The saline suppression test acutely expands intravascular volume (typically ~2 L over 4 hours) and can precipitate heart failure or severe hypertension — avoid in uncontrolled BP, cardiac failure or renal impairment, and use fludrocortisone/oral salt loading instead. Always correct dangerous hypokalaemia before any testing.
🎓 Remember the pattern: Conn's = HIGH aldosterone + LOW renin (raised ARR); secondary hyperaldosteronism = high aldosterone with HIGH renin. Aldosterone that fails to suppress after a saline load clinches the diagnosis.

Plasma free metanephrines and 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are the first-line biochemical screening tests for a catecholamine-secreting tumour — phaeochromocytoma (adrenal medulla) or paraganglioma (extra-adrenal sympathetic chain). They exploit a key metabolic fact: tumour cells continuously metabolise catecholamines to metanephrines inside the cell, so metanephrines leak steadily into the circulation even when catecholamine release is episodic, making them a more sensitive and specific marker than measuring adrenaline or noradrenaline directly.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Catecholamines are released in unpredictable bursts, so a single random catecholamine level is easily normal between paroxysms. Phaeochromocytomas, however, express catechol-O-methyltransferase and metabolise noradrenaline → normetadrenaline (normetanephrine) and adrenaline → metadrenaline (metanephrine) continuously and independently of secretion. These O-methylated metabolites spill into plasma and urine around the clock, giving a stable signal.

Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating (diaphoresis) and palpitations, often with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension.
Screen in: resistant/paroxysmal hypertension, adrenal incidentaloma, and hereditary syndromes — MEN2, von Hippel–Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1 and SDHx mutations.
Why metanephrines beat catecholamines: higher sensitivity (few false negatives) makes them the best rule-out test — normal metanephrines make phaeo very unlikely.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Two acceptable options, chosen by local availability and pre-test probability.

🩸Plasma free metanephrines
Highest sensitivity; best rule-out. Sample after ≥20–30 min supine rest.
🧪24h urinary fractionated metanephrines
High specificity; integrates output over a day. Needs complete, acidified collection.

Patient preparation to cut false positives:

Take plasma samples supine after rest (an upright, unrested sample raises sympathetic tone and normetanephrine); use age-adjusted, posture-specific reference ranges.
Avoid caffeine, nicotine, strenuous exercise and acute stress before sampling.
Review interfering drugs: tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs (e.g. venlafaxine), levodopa, and some antihypertensives (e.g. labetalol, sotalol interfering with assays) — withhold where clinically safe.
3INTERPRETATION

Interpret against the assay's upper reference limit ( URL); the degree of elevation drives the probability of a true tumour.

Metanephrines normal→Phaeochromocytoma effectively excluded (excellent negative predictive value)
Elevation >3–4× upper limit of normal→Strongly suggests phaeo/paraganglioma — proceed to localisation
Mild elevation (<3× ULN)→Often a false positive — recheck supine, remove interfering drugs/stress, repeat
Persistent borderline result→Clonidine suppression test can help — failure to suppress normetanephrine supports a tumour

Once biochemically confirmed, localise with CT or MRI of the adrenals/abdomen, adding functional imaging — 123I-MIBG or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET — particularly for extra-adrenal, multifocal, or metastatic disease.

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
False positives are the main problem: upright sampling, physiological stress (acute illness, critical care), caffeine, and drugs (TCAs, SNRIs, levodopa) inflate normetanephrine.
Never sequence backwards: do not image the adrenals first and act on an incidentaloma without biochemistry — but equally, do not dismiss a markedly elevated result as artefact.
Collection error (incomplete or non-acidified urine) invalidates urinary results; check creatinine to gauge adequacy.
🚩 Before ANY surgery or invasive procedure (including biopsy or induction of anaesthesia) for a confirmed phaeochromocytoma, establish alpha-blockade first (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) and add beta-blockade only afterwards. Unopposed beta-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a life-threatening hypertensive crisis.
🎓 Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive test, so a normal result is the strongest way to rule out phaeochromocytoma; the higher above the reference limit the value sits (>3–4×), the more likely the tumour is real rather than a stress- or drug-related false positive.

The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is a standardised dynamic test of the body's ability to handle a fixed glucose load. It is chiefly used to diagnose diabetes mellitus, impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and gestational diabetes, and — when paired with serial growth-hormone sampling — to confirm acromegaly. A weight-based measured glucose drink (75g in adults) is given after an overnight fast, and venous plasma glucose is measured fasting and again at 2 hours; the shape of the rise and, crucially, the 2-hour value reveal how effectively insulin secretion and action clear the load.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

A healthy person mounts a brisk insulin response that returns plasma glucose towards baseline within 2 hours. In diabetes and IGT this response is blunted or delayed, so glucose remains high at 2 hours — the abnormality the test unmasks.

Diagnosing diabetes when fasting glucose or HbA1c is equivocal, or when clinical suspicion is high despite borderline results.
Universal or risk-based screening for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks (earlier if previous GDM).
With growth-hormone sampling, to confirm acromegaly — glucose normally suppresses GH secretion.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
For 3 days beforehand the patient eats an unrestricted diet containing adequate carbohydrate (≥150g/day) — carbohydrate restriction falsely worsens tolerance.
Overnight fast of 8–14 hours; water only; no smoking during the test; remain seated and rested.
Draw fasting venous plasma glucose, then give 75g anhydrous glucose in ~300mL water, drunk over ~5 minutes.
Repeat plasma glucose at 2 hours. For acromegaly, sample GH at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes.
3INTERPRETATION (venous plasma glucose)
Fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L OR 2h ≥11.1 mmol/L→DIABETES MELLITUS
2h glucose 7.8–11.0 mmol/L→Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT)
Fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 mmol/L→Impaired fasting glucose (IFG)
Fasting <6.1 AND 2h <7.8 mmol/L→Normal glucose tolerance
Pregnancy: fasting ≥5.6 OR 2h ≥7.8 mmol/L (NICE)→GESTATIONAL DIABETES
Acromegaly: GH fails to suppress <0.4 µg/L (<1 mIU/L) after load→ACROMEGALY confirmed (paradoxical rise supports it)
🩸Fasting sample
Reflects hepatic glucose output / basal insulin
⏱️2-hour sample
Reflects peripheral glucose disposal
🍬75g load
Standardised anhydrous glucose challenge
🧬GH sampling
Add-on for acromegaly (suppression test)
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Poor reproducibility — day-to-day variation is high, so results can be inconsistent.
Confounded by acute illness, prolonged bed rest, and drugs (corticosteroids, thiazides, beta-agonists) that impair tolerance.
Not used in acute metabolic decompensation — diagnose overt hyperglycaemia directly instead.
Nausea or vomiting of the drink invalidates the test.
🚩 A single abnormal value in an asymptomatic person must be confirmed by a repeat test on a different day before labelling diabetes — only symptomatic patients can be diagnosed on one result. Never do an OGTT during acute illness, and be alert that undiagnosed diabetes may present in crisis (DKA/HHS) requiring emergency treatment, not a tolerance test.
🎓 In acromegaly the OGTT is read the opposite way to diabetes: you want to see GH suppress. Failure of GH to fall below 0.4 µg/L — or a paradoxical rise — confirms the diagnosis. Remember GDM has the lowest thresholds (fasting ≥5.6, 2h ≥7.8), because tighter control protects the fetus.

The 72-hour supervised fast is the gold-standard provocation test for endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, most importantly insulinoma. Its logic is simple: in a healthy person, a falling blood glucose switches insulin OFF, but an insulinoma secretes insulin autonomously and cannot be suppressed. The diagnosis is framed by Whipple's triad — symptoms of hypoglycaemia, a simultaneously LOW measured plasma glucose, and relief of symptoms once glucose is given.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to investigate unexplained fasting (post-absorptive) hypoglycaemia where endogenous hyperinsulinism is suspected. Prolonged fasting drives glucose down; the physiological response is insulin suppression, a switch to lipolysis, and rising ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate). An insulinoma keeps insulin inappropriately high, which both keeps glucose low AND suppresses ketogenesis — so the hallmark is hypoglycaemia with LOW ketones.

Aim: demonstrate hypoglycaemia with inappropriately non-suppressed insulin.
Whipple's triad must be satisfied to call the result clinically significant.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A supervised inpatient fast of up to 72 hours. Only calorie-free, caffeine-free fluids are allowed; non-essential medications are stopped. Note the exact start time (last calorie intake). Capillary and venous glucose are checked regularly (e.g. 4–6 hourly, then more frequently as glucose falls).

When blood glucose falls to ≤2.5 mmol/L (or the patient develops symptoms/signs of neuroglycopenia), take paired samples at the same moment for:

🩸Glucose
lab (not just capillary) to confirm true hypoglycaemia
🧪Insulin
should be suppressed — if not, hyperinsulinism
🔗C-peptide
marks ENDOGENOUS insulin secretion
🧬Proinsulin
raised in insulinoma
💊Sulphonylurea screen
excludes drug-induced hyperinsulinism
🔥β-hydroxybutyrate
LOW in hyperinsulinism (insulin blocks ketogenesis)

The fast is terminated at 72 h, when Whipple's triad is demonstrated with a confirmed low glucose, or earlier for significant neuroglycopenia. At termination (before glucose is given) a final paired sample is taken, then 1 mg IV glucagon may be given with glucose measured at 10, 20 and 30 min (a rise >1.4 mmol/L suggests preserved hepatic glycogen driven by insulin excess). Hypoglycaemia is then treated.

3INTERPRETATION (at the time of hypoglycaemia)

Interpret ONLY on the sample drawn when lab glucose is ≤2.2–2.5 mmol/L. The diagnostic picture of endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma) is:

Glucose ≤2.2 mmol/L + insulin ≥3 µU/mL (≥18 pmol/L)→inappropriately non-suppressed insulin = hyperinsulinism
C-peptide ≥0.2 nmol/L (≥0.6 ng/mL)→insulin is ENDOGENOUS (pancreatic) → insulinoma likely
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma→localise (CT/MRI pancreas + endoscopic ultrasound; selective venous sampling if occult) → surgical enucleation/resection (diazoxide to control hypoglycaemia if unresectable or pre-operatively)
Proinsulin ≥5 pmol/L→supports insulinoma
β-hydroxybutyrate ≤2.7 mmol/L (LOW)→insulin suppressing ketogenesis → hyperinsulinism (not fasting ketosis)
Fast completes 72 h with glucose staying normal & insulin suppressed→insulinoma effectively excluded

C-peptide is the key discriminator — it separates the causes of hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia:

High insulin + HIGH C-peptide + high proinsulin, drug screen negative→INSULINOMA (endogenous)
High insulin + LOW / suppressed C-peptide→EXOGENOUS insulin (factitious / accidental)
High insulin + HIGH C-peptide + POSITIVE sulphonylurea screen→SULPHONYLUREA use / abuse
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Confirm with LAB glucose: capillary meters are unreliable at low readings — never diagnose on a bedside stick alone.
Timing is everything: insulin/C-peptide are only meaningful when drawn simultaneously with a truly low glucose; a "high" insulin at normal glucose is uninterpretable.
Miss the sulphonylurea: without a drug screen, sulphonylurea abuse mimics insulinoma exactly (identical high insulin + high C-peptide).
Resource-intensive: requires inpatient supervision; ~1/3 of insulinomas need the full 72 h to declare, so a short negative fast does not exclude the diagnosis.
🚩 This test deliberately provokes hypoglycaemia and must be closely supervised with IV access ready. Terminate the fast immediately for neuroglycopenia (confusion, drowsiness, seizures, focal deficit) — but take the diagnostic paired sample BEFORE administering glucose/glucagon, otherwise the whole test is wasted. Treat promptly, then confirm glucose recovery.
🎓 Remember the triad of samples at the moment of hypoglycaemia: insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin (plus ketones and a sulphonylurea screen). C-peptide is the single most discriminating result — HIGH points to the pancreas (insulinoma or sulphonylurea), LOW/suppressed points to injected exogenous insulin.

The water deprivation test is a dynamic endocrine investigation used to differentiate the causes of polyuria and polydipsia (passing large volumes of dilute urine with excessive thirst). It distinguishes cranial (central) diabetes insipidus (deficient ADH secretion), nephrogenic DI (renal resistance to ADH) and primary polydipsia (compulsive/psychogenic water drinking) by observing whether the kidney can concentrate urine when fluid is withheld, and then whether it responds to exogenous ADH (desmopressin).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Performed to establish the cause of confirmed hypotonic polyuria (typically >3 L/day of dilute urine) once osmotic diuresis (e.g. hyperglycaemia) and hypercalcaemia/hypokalaemia have been excluded. The principle exploits ADH (vasopressin) physiology: rising plasma osmolality should stimulate ADH release, which acts on renal collecting-duct V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 channels, reabsorbing water and concentrating the urine. Depriving fluid raises plasma osmolality; a healthy kidney with intact ADH concentrates the urine, whereas any lesion in ADH secretion or action fails to do so.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
The patient empties their bladder and all fluids are withheld (food may be allowed dry). Phase 1 (deprivation): over ~8 hours, measure body weight, plasma osmolality and urine osmolality hourly. Phase 2 (desmopressin/DDAVP): once plasma osmolality has risen or urine fails to concentrate, give desmopressin (2 µg IM/SC, or ~20 µg intranasally), then allow fluid and continue measuring urine osmolality for a further 2–4 hours. Copeptin (the stable C-terminal fragment of the ADH precursor) may be assayed as a newer, more robust surrogate marker of endogenous ADH secretion.
Start early morning after a normal overnight; supervise continuously.
Weigh accurately at baseline — weight loss guides safe stopping.
Paired plasma and urine osmolality are the key measurements.
3INTERPRETATION
Judge the deprivation response first, then the DDAVP response. A concentrated urine osmolality of >600–800 mOsm/kg after deprivation excludes significant DI.
Deprivation: urine osmolality >600–800 mOsm/kg, plasma stays normal→Normal / primary polydipsia (kidney concentrates — no DDAVP needed)
Deprivation: urine stays dilute (<300) & plasma osmolality rises — THEN DDAVP: urine concentrates (>600–800 / rises >50%)→Cranial (central) DI — responds to exogenous ADH
Deprivation: urine stays dilute & plasma rises — THEN DDAVP: urine STAYS dilute (little/no rise)→Nephrogenic DI — kidneys resistant to ADH
Deprivation: urine concentrates but only partially (may plateau <600)→Primary polydipsia with medullary washout (or partial DI — interpret with copeptin)
🧠Cranial DI
Deprivation: dilute (fails). DDAVP: concentrates. Deficient ADH.
🫘Nephrogenic DI
Deprivation: dilute (fails). DDAVP: still dilute. ADH resistance.
💧Primary polydipsia
Deprivation: concentrates (may be partial from washout). ADH intact.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Medullary washout: chronic polyuria dilutes the renal medulla, blunting concentrating ability and mimicking partial DI — a common cause of an equivocal result.
Surreptitious drinking: a patient with primary polydipsia who drinks during the test invalidates it — hence continuous supervision.
Partial forms: partial cranial and partial nephrogenic DI give intermediate responses; copeptin (baseline and post-hypertonic-saline stimulation) now improves discrimination and is more reliable than the classic test.
🚩 STOP the test if body weight falls by >3% (or >5%), or if plasma sodium/osmolality rises above the normal range — the patient risks dangerous hypernatraemic dehydration and hypovolaemia. Continuous close supervision is mandatory; never leave the patient unmonitored or allow unrestricted access to fluids.
🎓 Remember the two-step logic: deprivation separates DI from primary polydipsia (concentrators vs failures), and DDAVP then separates cranial DI (concentrates) from nephrogenic DI (no response). A useful mnemonic — cranial craves the desmopressin and responds; nephrogenic neglects it.
SPECIAL TESTS__GI Absorption & Breath Te:
The Schilling test is a classic, now largely historical, radioisotope study used to determine the cause of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency once deficiency is confirmed. It cannot tell you whether a patient is B12 deficient — it distinguishes why they cannot absorb it, separating lack of intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy) from terminal ileal disease and bacterial overgrowth. It has been largely replaced by intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies plus clinical assessment, but remains a favourite exam topic for testing physiology.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Used to establish the mechanism of a confirmed low serum B12. Dietary B12 requires gastric intrinsic factor (IF), secreted by parietal cells, to form a complex absorbed at receptors in the terminal ileum. The test exploits this pathway: radiolabelled oral B12 that is successfully absorbed enters the blood and, because binding sites are pre-saturated, spills into the urine where it can be measured. Failure of any step — IF secretion, ileal uptake, or competition by gut bacteria — reduces urinary excretion.
Confirms the site of the absorptive defect, not the deficiency itself.
Depends on the physiology of the gastric IF – terminal ileum axis.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Give an oral dose of radiolabelled B12 (e.g. 57Co-cobalamin). One to two hours later give a large intramuscular (IM) loading dose of unlabelled B12 (~1000 µg). This IM dose saturates the plasma and hepatic B12-binding proteins so that any labelled B12 that is absorbed is not retained but is excreted in the urine. A complete 24-hour urine collection is then made and the fraction of the labelled dose excreted is measured. The study is done in stages, each modifying one variable to localise the defect.
Patient should be fasted before the oral dose; the IM flushing dose is essential.
Accurate, complete urine collection over the full 24 h is critical to validity.
3STAGES & INTERPRETATION
Normal urinary excretion is ≥10% of the oral labelled dose over 24 h; a value <10% (often quoted as <7%) indicates malabsorption. Each successive stage adds one corrective factor to see what normalises the result.
STAGE 1: oral labelled B12 alone → LOW excretion→B12 malabsorption confirmed — cause not yet localised
STAGE 2: repeat WITH oral intrinsic factor → excretion NORMALISES→Defect was lack of IF = PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA (or gastrectomy)
Pernicious anaemia / gastrectomy confirmed→lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin replacement. B12 & folate ›
STAGE 2: with IF but excretion STAYS LOW→Terminal ileal disease (Crohn's, ileal resection) or bacterial overgrowth
STAGE 3: repeat after a course of ANTIBIOTICS → excretion corrects→Small bowel BACTERIAL OVERGROWTH is the cause
STAGE 3: no correction after antibiotics→Primary terminal ileal pathology (e.g. Crohn's, resection)
🧪Stage 1
Oral labelled B12 alone — screens for malabsorption (low = abnormal).
💊Stage 2
Adds oral intrinsic factor — corrects in pernicious anaemia / gastrectomy.
🦠Stage 3
Adds antibiotics — corrects in small bowel bacterial overgrowth.
🔬No correction
Persistently low despite IF & antibiotics → terminal ileal disease.
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
The test is only valid with normal renal function, because it relies on urinary excretion — impaired GFR delays excretion and produces a falsely low result. An incomplete 24-hour urine collection is the commonest reason for a spuriously abnormal answer. It requires radioisotope handling and has been superseded in modern UK practice by serum IF and parietal cell antibodies, holotranscobalamin and clinical assessment.
The IM flushing dose can itself begin to treat the deficiency — interpret before starting long-term replacement.
Combined stage kits (labelled B12 with and without IF given together) reduced patient burden.
🚩 Results are invalid in renal impairment (delayed urinary excretion mimics malabsorption) and in any patient who fails to complete an accurate 24-hour urine collection — always confirm normal renal function and collection compliance before interpreting a low value.
🎓 Remember the logic by what corrects the excretion: corrects with intrinsic factor → pernicious anaemia; corrects with antibiotics → bacterial overgrowth; corrects with neither → terminal ileal disease (Crohn's / resection).

Lactose tolerance / intolerance testing investigates suspected lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance) in a patient with bloating, watery diarrhoea, flatulence and crampy abdominal pain arising 30 min–2 h after milk or dairy. The tests exploit one principle: without brush-border lactase, dietary lactose is not split into glucose + galactose, so it passes undigested into the colon where bacteria ferment it — generating hydrogen gas and drawing in fluid osmotically. The lactose hydrogen breath test is the most widely used non-invasive method.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Used to confirm lactose malabsorption in patients with dairy-triggered GI symptoms, or to explain persistent symptoms after gastroenteritis or in coeliac disease.
Biochemical basis: lactase (a brush-border disaccharidase) hydrolyses lactose → glucose + galactose for absorption. Deficiency → osmotic load + colonic bacterial fermentation.
🧬Primary hypolactasia
Adult-onset, genetically programmed decline in lactase (LCT gene) — common, especially non-Northern-European ancestry
🦠Secondary hypolactasia
Transient mucosal damage — post-gastroenteritis, coeliac disease, Crohn’s; often reversible once mucosa heals
👶Congenital alactasia
Rare autosomal-recessive absence of lactase from birth — severe neonatal diarrhoea
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Preparation: overnight fast; avoid antibiotics, laxatives and high-fibre/fermentable foods beforehand; no smoking or vigorous exercise (both alter breath H₂); good oral hygiene / mouthwash to reduce oral bacteria.
Lactose load: oral lactose (commonly 25–50 g in adults, or 1–2 g/kg) dissolved in water.
💨Hydrogen breath test
Baseline breath sample, then end-expiratory breath H₂ measured every 15–30 min for 2–3 h
🩸Blood tolerance test
Serial venous glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min after the lactose load
🔬Biopsy / genetic
Duodenal/jejunal biopsy lactase assay (gold standard) or LCT (C/T-13910) polymorphism genotyping
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
Breath H₂ rise ≥20 ppm above baseline→Positive — lactose malabsorption (colonic fermentation of undigested lactose)
Breath H₂ rise <20 ppm + no symptoms→Negative — lactase activity adequate, malabsorption excluded
Blood glucose rise <1.1 mmol/L (<20 mg/dL) — flat curve→Lactose not digested to glucose + galactose = lactase deficiency
Blood glucose rise ≥1.1 mmol/L (≥20 mg/dL)→Normal digestion — lactase deficiency excluded
Reproduction of symptoms (bloating, diarrhoea, wind) during test→Supports clinical lactose intolerance, not just malabsorption
Positive (lactose intolerance)→dietary lactose restriction ± lactase supplements; safeguard calcium/vitamin D; if secondary, treat the mucosal cause (it is reversible)
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO): bacteria in the small bowel ferment lactose early, producing an early H₂ rise — a false-positive for lactose malabsorption.
Non-hydrogen (methane) producers: ~10–15% of people harbour methanogenic flora that consume H₂, giving a false-negative breath test; measuring methane concurrently improves accuracy.
Recent antibiotics, laxatives, delayed gastric emptying and diabetes/impaired glucose handling can distort results; the blood test is less specific because glucose homeostasis affects the curve.
🚩 A positive test confirms lactose malabsorption, not the cause. In a patient with weight loss, anaemia or refractory symptoms, do NOT stop at “lactose intolerance” — exclude coeliac disease and other mucosal pathology, since secondary hypolactasia is a marker of underlying small-bowel disease.
🎓 Remember the discordant directions: in malabsorption breath hydrogen goes UP (≥20 ppm) while blood glucose stays FLAT (<1.1 mmol/L). A helpful bedside step — a symptom-and-diet diary with a trial of lactose exclusion followed by rechallenge — is often used before or instead of formal testing.

Breath tests are non-invasive, exploiting the fact that specific gases in exhaled air are generated by processes not native to human metabolism. Two are commonly examined: the hydrogen (± methane) breath test for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and carbohydrate malabsorption, and the urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori. Both depend on collecting serial or timed breath samples after an oral substrate.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Hydrogen/methane test: human cells cannot produce hydrogen — only gut bacteria ferment carbohydrate to H₂ (and some archaea to methane). A fermentable substrate is swallowed; gas diffuses into blood and is exhaled, so a rise in breath H₂ is a direct marker of bacterial fermentation. Used for SIBO and for lactose/fructose malabsorption.
Urea breath test: H. pylori produces abundant urease. Swallowed ¹³C- (or ¹⁴C-) labelled urea is split by the enzyme into labelled CO₂, which is absorbed and exhaled. Detecting labelled CO₂ confirms active infection, both at diagnosis and to confirm eradication.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED & PREPARATION
Hydrogen/methane: after an overnight fast, a baseline breath sample is taken, then an oral substrate is given — glucose (75 g) or lactulose for SIBO, or the relevant sugar (lactose/fructose) for malabsorption. Breath H₂ (± CH₄) is sampled every 15–20 min for 2–3 hours. Preparation: avoid antibiotics for ~4 weeks, avoid fermentable/high-fibre foods the day before, and no smoking or exercise around testing.
Urea breath test: fast for ~6 hours, take a baseline breath sample, swallow labelled urea (often with a citric acid drink to delay gastric emptying), then collect a breath sample at ~30 min for the labelled-CO₂ ratio.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
H₂ rise ≥20 ppm above baseline within ~90 min→EARLY rise before substrate reaches colon — suggests SIBO
Positive (SIBO)→treat with rifaximin (or rotating antibiotics) and correct the underlying cause (dysmotility, blind loop, anatomy); replace B12 and fat-soluble vitamins
Symptomatic H₂ rise ≥20 ppm after lactose→Lactose malabsorption
Late single peak (only as substrate reaches colon)→Normal colonic fermentation — not SIBO
Flat H₂ trace throughout→Non-producer (methane) or recent antibiotics — possible false negative
Labelled CO₂ above lab threshold (e.g. Δ≥4‰)→Active H. pylori infection (positive urea breath test)
Labelled CO₂ below threshold after treatment→Successful eradication confirmed
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
🧪Methane producers
~15% harbour methanogens — measure CH₄ too or H₂ test falsely negative
⏱️Rapid transit
Fast small-bowel transit lets substrate reach colon early, mimicking a SIBO peak
💊Recent antibiotics
Suppress flora — false-negative hydrogen and urea breath tests
🧴PPIs / bismuth
Suppress H. pylori urease — false-negative urea breath test
🚩 The urea breath test is only valid off interfering drugs: stop PPIs for 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth for 4 weeks before testing (and allow ≥4 weeks after eradication therapy before a test of cure), otherwise suppressed bacterial load gives a false-negative result and infection is missed.
🎓 An early breath-hydrogen rise (≥20 ppm within ~90 min) points to SIBO, whereas a single late peak is normal colonic fermentation. Remember hydrogen comes only from bacteria, and the urea breath test detects active H. pylori via urease — making it the preferred non-invasive test of eradication.

The sweat chloride test is the gold-standard diagnostic investigation for cystic fibrosis (CF). CF is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which encodes a cyclic-AMP-regulated chloride channel. In the sweat gland duct, defective CFTR prevents reabsorption of chloride (and secondarily sodium) from the primary sweat, so the sweat that reaches the skin surface is abnormally salty — a high sweat chloride concentration is the biochemical hallmark of the disease.

1Indication & principle

The test is performed to confirm CF after a positive newborn bloodspot screen (raised immunoreactive trypsinogen, IRT) or when there is clinical suspicion.

Newborn screening: raised IRT flags possible CF and triggers confirmatory testing.
Clinical clues: recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea and pancreatic insufficiency, failure to thrive.
Also: meconium ileus in neonates, and male infertility (congenital absence of the vas deferens).

Biochemical basis: normally CFTR reabsorbs Cl⁻ from sweat as it passes up the duct, with Na⁺ following. In CF this channel fails, so both ions remain in the sweat → a high surface chloride concentration, which is what the test measures.

2How it is performed

Pilocarpine iontophoresis is used to stimulate localised sweating, followed by collection and quantitative chloride measurement.

A small skin area (usually the forearm) is cleaned; pilocarpine is driven into the skin by a weak electric current (iontophoresis) to stimulate the local sweat glands.
Sweat is collected over ~30 minutes onto pre-weighed filter paper/gauze or into a Macroduct coil.
The sample is analysed for chloride concentration (the diagnostic analyte); an adequate sweat volume/weight is essential for a valid result.

Usually best performed once the infant is ≥2 weeks old and >3 kg, to ensure sufficient sweat can be collected.

3Interpretation & cut-offs

Results are interpreted using established sweat chloride bands:

Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L→Diagnostic of / consistent with CF
Sweat chloride 30–59 mmol/L→Intermediate/borderline — repeat test and proceed to CFTR genetic testing
Sweat chloride <30 mmol/L→CF unlikely

A result in the diagnostic or intermediate range should be confirmed with CFTR genetic (mutation) testing, and a positive test is ideally repeated on a separate occasion.

4Pitfalls & limitations
💧Inadequate sample
Insufficient sweat volume/weight (common in neonates <2 weeks or low weight) gives an unreliable result → repeat.
🧪False positives
Rare causes of raised sweat chloride include malnutrition, untreated hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and some skin conditions (e.g. eczema).
🧬Confirm genetically
Sweat chloride does not identify the mutation; diagnosis is confirmed with CFTR genetic testing.
🚩 An inadequate sweat sample (too little sweat collected) must NOT be reported as normal — it is a failed test and must be repeated. Under-collection is especially likely in neonates <2 weeks old or of low weight; a spuriously low value here could falsely reassure and delay a CF diagnosis.
🎓 Remember the key number: sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L is diagnostic, 30–59 mmol/L is borderline (repeat + genetics), <30 mmol/L makes CF unlikely. It is chloride — not sodium — that is measured for the diagnostic cut-offs.

Faecal elastase-1 is the standard screen for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI). Elastase is a pancreas-specific enzyme that is not degraded during intestinal transit, so its concentration in a single stool sample reflects pancreatic enzyme output — low levels indicate the pancreas is not secreting enough enzyme to digest food.

1When to use it
Chronic steatorrhoea/malabsorption, weight loss, or fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Suspected chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or pancreatic cancer.
2Interpretation
> 200 µg/g→normal exocrine function
100–200 µg/g→mild–moderate exocrine insufficiency
< 100 µg/g→severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
Unaffected by ongoing PERT (it measures native pancreatic elastase) — no need to stop enzyme supplements. A watery/diluted stool can give a falsely low result.
3What to do next
Low faecal elastase (EPI)→start pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT / Creon) with meals and replace fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); investigate the cause (imaging for chronic pancreatitis / pancreatic cancer). Chronic pancreatitis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Faecal elastase is the finals screen for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: <100 µg/g = severe → PERT + fat-soluble vitamins. It stays valid on enzyme supplements, so you do not stop PERT to test.
SPECIAL TESTS__Respiratory & Sleep:
The Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA / QuantiFERON-TB) and the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux) are immunological tests for infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Both detect a host memory T-cell response to mycobacterial antigens and are used principally to diagnose latent TB infection (LTBI) — and as an adjunct where active TB is suspected. Crucially, neither test distinguishes latent from active TB: a positive result confirms infection at some point, but the latent-versus-active question is answered clinically and radiologically, not by these assays.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to screen for latent TB: contacts of infectious cases, new entrants from high-incidence countries, before starting immunosuppression (e.g. anti-TNF-α biologics), in healthcare workers, and in HIV-positive individuals. Both rely on cell-mediated (type IV) immunity — memory T-cells primed by prior TB exposure recognise mycobacterial antigens and mount a response.

IGRA: a blood sample is incubated with M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10); sensitised T-cells release interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), which is quantified (QuantiFERON) or the responding cells counted (T-SPOT).
TST/Mantoux: intradermal purified protein derivative (PPD) elicits a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction (induration) if the person is sensitised.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
IGRA: a single venous blood draw into specialised tubes (nil/control, TB antigen, mitogen positive-control). Incubated, then IFN-γ measured by ELISA. One visit only — no need for the patient to return.
TST/Mantoux: 0.1 mL of PPD (2 TU) injected intradermally into the volar forearm, raising a bleb. The patient must return at 48–72 hours so the transverse diameter of induration (not erythema) is measured in mm.
🎓 A key practical advantage of IGRA: because ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are absent from the BCG strain and from most environmental (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria, IGRA is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination, whereas the TST is.
3INTERPRETATION
IGRA positive→TB infection present (latent OR active) — assess clinically/radiologically to distinguish
Latent TB (active excluded: asymptomatic, normal CXR, negative sputum)→treat latent TB — 3 months isoniazid + rifampicin (or 6 months isoniazid), and always before anti-TNF / immunosuppression. Tuberculosis ›
IGRA negative→TB infection unlikely (does not fully exclude — beware immunosuppression)
IGRA indeterminate→Failed mitogen positive control or high nil (anergy/technical) — repeat
TST induration ≥ 5 mm→Positive in high-risk groups (HIV, immunosuppressed, recent close contacts)
TST induration ≥ 15 mm→Positive regardless of BCG status (strongly suggests infection)
TST / Mantoux ≥ 5 mm induration→Positive by current UK (NICE) guidance, regardless of BCG history — the older 6/15 mm thresholds are superseded
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
🧪ESAT-6
TB-specific antigen; absent from BCG
🧪CFP-10
TB-specific antigen; absent from BCG
⚠️Anergy
Immunosuppression → false negative
🩹BCG
False-positive TST only, not IGRA
Neither test tells you if disease is active — sputum microscopy/culture, NAAT and imaging (CXR) are needed for active TB.
TST requires two visits, is operator-dependent to read, and can boost on repeat testing.
🚩 Neither IGRA nor TST can distinguish latent from active TB, and both may be falsely negative in immunosuppression/anergy (e.g. HIV, corticosteroids, anti-TNF therapy) or in overwhelming active disease. A negative result must never be used to exclude active TB in a symptomatic or immunocompromised patient — proceed to sputum culture, NAAT and imaging.

Pleural fluid analysis is the bedside-to-laboratory work-up of fluid aspirated from a pleural effusion by pleural aspiration (thoracocentesis). Its first job is to separate a transudate (a filtration problem from raised hydrostatic or reduced oncotic pressure) from an exudate (a leak from raised capillary permeability due to inflammation, infection or malignancy), because that single split reshapes the whole differential. Light's criteria are the validated rule that makes the call, and a small panel of additional tests then narrows the cause and flags effusions that need urgent drainage.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Any newly-diagnosed unilateral effusion, or a bilateral effusion that does not settle with treatment of the presumed cause, warrants diagnostic aspiration. The principle is biochemical: capillaries in transudative states stay intact and hold back large molecules, so the fluid is protein- and LDH-poor. In exudative states the inflamed or invaded pleura leaks protein and cellular contents (LDH), so the fluid concentrations rise toward those of serum. Comparing fluid with a paired serum sample quantifies that leak.
Transudate — systemic imbalance, pleura is a passive bystander; effusions are often bilateral.
Exudate — local pleural pathology; effusions are more often unilateral.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Ultrasound-guided aspiration is standard: the patient sits leaning forward over a table, and a needle is passed above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. Send a paired serum sample for protein and LDH at the same sitting so the ratios can be calculated. Distribute the fluid into the correct containers: a plain/biochemistry tube (protein, LDH, glucose), a blood-gas syringe processed promptly (pH), a sterile pot (microbiology — Gram stain, culture, AFB, adenosine deaminase), and a cytology pot (malignant cells, differential cell count). Add amylase or triglycerides when the clinical picture suggests it.
pH sample→collect anaerobically in a blood-gas syringe & analyse promptly; avoid lidocaine contamination which falsely lowers pH
3INTERPRETATION — LIGHT'S CRITERIA
The fluid is an exudate if ANY ONE criterion is met; if none are met it is a transudate.
Pleural protein / serum protein > 0.5→EXUDATE
Pleural LDH / serum LDH > 0.6→EXUDATE
Pleural LDH > ⅔ of upper limit of normal serum LDH→EXUDATE
None of the three met→TRANSUDATE — pursue systemic causes
Additional analytes refine the cause:
pH < 7.2 in infected/parapneumonic fluid→complicated effusion/empyema — mandates chest-drain insertion
Low glucose (< 3.3 mmol/L)→empyema, TB, rheumatoid, malignancy
Raised adenosine deaminase / lymphocyte-rich fluid→tuberculous effusion
Pleural amylase raised→pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture
Triglycerides > 1.24 mmol/L, milky fluid→chylothorax (thoracic duct disruption)
4CAUSES — TRANSUDATE vs EXUDATE
💧Heart failure
TRANSUDATE — raised pulmonary venous/hydrostatic pressure; commonest transudate
🫀Cirrhosis
TRANSUDATE — low albumin + hepatic hydrothorax
🧫Nephrotic / hypoalbuminaemia
TRANSUDATE — reduced plasma oncotic pressure
🦠Parapneumonic / empyema
EXUDATE — infection; check pH/glucose, may need drainage
🎗️Malignancy
EXUDATE — send cytology; often blood-stained, may reaccumulate
🫁Tuberculosis
EXUDATE — lymphocytic, raised ADA, low glucose
🩸Pulmonary embolism
EXUDATE (occasionally transudate) — infarction/permeability
⚗️Pancreatitis / connective tissue
EXUDATE — raised amylase (pancreatitis); RA/SLE serositis
🚩 In a parapneumonic effusion, pleural fluid pH < 7.2 (or frank pus/positive Gram stain/organisms on culture) defines a complicated effusion or empyema and mandates prompt intercostal chest-drain insertion plus antibiotics — antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay worsens outcome.
🎓 Light's criteria are highly sensitive but can mislabel a transudate as an exudate in heart failure treated with diuretics (diuresis concentrates fluid protein/LDH). If the clinical picture is transudative but Light's says exudate, calculate the serum-effusion albumin gradient: a gradient > 12 g/L (1.2 g/dL) reclassifies the fluid as a transudate.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is a procedure performed during flexible bronchoscopy in which the scope is wedged into a subsegmental bronchus, sequential aliquots of warmed sterile isotonic saline are instilled and re-aspirated, and the returned fluid is sent to sample the cells, proteins and microorganisms lining the distal airways and alveoli. It is the key bronchoscopic tool for diagnosing pulmonary infection in the immunocompromised host and for characterising diffuse parenchymal (interstitial) lung disease, alveolar haemorrhage and eosinophilic/proteinosis syndromes.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Wedging the bronchoscope and instilling saline effectively ‘washes out’ the epithelial lining fluid of ~10⁶ alveoli, providing a liquid biopsy of the distal lung without cutting tissue.

Infection in the immunocompromised (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy): the leading indication — sample for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), fungi (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus), mycobacteria and respiratory viruses.
Interstitial lung disease (ILD) characterisation and to exclude infection/malignancy before immunosuppression.
Suspected diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, eosinophilic pneumonia and alveolar proteinosis.
🦠Infection (immunosuppressed)
PCP, fungi, mycobacteria, viruses — microscopy, culture, PCR, silver stain
🩸Alveolar haemorrhage
Progressively bloodier aliquots + haemosiderin-laden macrophages
🫧Alveolar proteinosis
Milky/opaque effluent, PAS-positive amorphous material
🔬ILD phenotyping
Differential cell count guides sarcoid vs HP vs eosinophilic disease
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Preparation: informed consent, fasting, topical lidocaine + light sedation; check platelets/clotting and oxygenation. Withhold high bleeding-risk anticoagulants per local protocol.
Site: wedge the bronchoscope in a subsegment of the affected lobe — the right middle lobe or lingula for diffuse disease (best return), or the radiologically abnormal segment for focal disease.
Instil & aspirate: warmed sterile 0.9% saline in aliquots (typically 3–5 × 20–60 mL, ~100–240 mL total), gently re-aspirated after each. A return of ≥30% of instilled volume is adequate.
Handle sample: the first (‘bronchial’) aliquot is often discarded/analysed separately; pooled fluid is sent promptly for cytology/differential count, microscopy, culture, PCR and special stains (Grocott/silver for PCP).
3INTERPRETATION — BAL DIFFERENTIAL CELL COUNT

A normal BAL differential is dominated by alveolar macrophages (>80–85%), with lymphocytes <10–15%, neutrophils <3% and eosinophils <1%. The dominant abnormal cell line, together with the CD4:CD8 ratio, narrows the differential.

LYMPHOCYTOSIS + raised CD4:CD8 (>4)→Sarcoidosis
LYMPHOCYTOSIS + low CD4:CD8→Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (often marked lymphocytosis)
NEUTROPHILIA→Infection, IPF, ARDS
EOSINOPHILIA (≥25% → eosinophilic pneumonia)→Eosinophilic pneumonia, drug reaction
Progressively bloodier aliquots + haemosiderin-laden macrophages→Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Milky effluent, PAS-positive amorphous material→Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
Silver/Grocott stain or PCR positive for cysts→Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
PCP confirmed on BAL→high-dose co-trimoxazole, adding corticosteroids if hypoxic (PaO₂ <9.3 kPa or SpO₂ <92% on air)
🧫Lymphocytosis
Sarcoid (high CD4:CD8) · HP (low CD4:CD8)
⚔️Neutrophilia
Infection · IPF · ARDS
🌸Eosinophilia
Eosinophilic pneumonia · drug reaction
🩸Haemosiderin macrophages
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Cell patterns are supportive, not pathognomonic — always integrate with clinical picture, HRCT and serology; overlap is common.
Poor return (emphysema, poor wedge) and contamination from the proximal airways (upper-airway flora, oropharyngeal cells) degrade the sample.
Transient post-procedure fever and a self-limiting drop in FEV₁/gas exchange are expected; new focal infiltrate on the lavaged segment can mimic infection.
🚩 BAL causes transient hypoxaemia and desaturation, bleeding, post-procedure fever/infection and bronchospasm. Avoid or use extreme caution in severe hypoxaemia (e.g. cannot maintain SpO₂ despite supplemental O₂), the haemodynamically unstable patient, uncontrolled arrhythmia, recent MI, or uncorrected bleeding diathesis — the fluid load can precipitate acute respiratory deterioration.
🎓 A markedly raised BAL CD4:CD8 ratio (>3.5–4) is highly specific for sarcoidosis, whereas a low CD4:CD8 with intense lymphocytosis points to hypersensitivity pneumonitis — a classic exam discriminator between the two granulomatous lymphocytic diseases.

Polysomnography (PSG) and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) are the paired tools used to investigate suspected obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and other sleep disorders. The ESS quantifies subjective daytime sleepiness; the sleep study objectively measures breathing, oxygenation and sleep architecture overnight, generating the apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) that grades OSA severity and guides treatment.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Investigation is prompted by a clinical picture of loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, choking/gasping arousals and excessive daytime somnolence, typically in an obese, middle-aged patient. Associated flags include resistant hypertension, a large collar size and a crowded oropharynx.

In OSA, repetitive pharyngeal collapse causes apnoeas (airflow cessation) and hypopnoeas (partial reduction), each terminated by a cortical arousal → fragmented, non-restorative sleep.
Recurrent desaturation–reoxygenation drives sympathetic surges, contributing to hypertension and cardiovascular risk.
The ESS is a validated first-step questionnaire scoring the likelihood of dozing in 8 everyday situations (e.g. sitting reading, watching TV, as a car passenger), each rated 0–3, total 0–24.
ESS > 10–11 / 24→Excessive daytime sleepiness — warrants objective sleep study
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

For suspected uncomplicated OSA, a home limited-channel cardiorespiratory (respiratory) polygraphy is usually first-line: it records airflow, respiratory effort and oximetry without EEG. Full attended polysomnography (in a sleep laboratory) is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected non-respiratory sleep disorders, and adds neurophysiology for formal sleep staging.

🧠EEG
Sleep staging (N1–N3, REM) and arousals
👁️EOG
Eye movements — identifies REM sleep
💪EMG
Chin/limb tone; REM atonia, limb movements
❤️ECG
Heart rate & arrhythmias during events
💨Airflow
Nasal pressure/thermistor — detects apnoea/hypopnoea
🎗️Effort bands
Chest & abdominal effort; distinguishes obstructive vs central
🩸Pulse oximetry
SpO₂ — desaturations quantify the ODI
3INTERPRETATION — AHI & ODI

The key output is the apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) = number of apnoeas + hypopnoeas per hour of sleep. The oxygen desaturation index (ODI) counts SpO₂ drops (typically ≥ 3–4%) per hour and is the main metric on limited home studies. In obstructive events, effort bands continue to move despite absent airflow; in central events, effort is absent.

AHI 5–15 /hr→Mild OSA
AHI 15–30 /hr→Moderate OSA
AHI > 30 /hr→Severe OSA
Effort persists, airflow absent→Obstructive event (vs central = no effort)

OSA syndrome (OSAS) is diagnosed when an abnormal AHI is combined with symptoms such as daytime sleepiness. Management is offered along a spectrum from conservative to device-based.

Lifestyle: weight loss, alcohol/sedative avoidance, smoking cessation, positional advice.
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is first-line for moderate–severe OSA and symptomatic mild disease; mandibular advancement devices are an alternative in milder cases.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Limited home polygraphy lacks EEG, so it cannot measure true sleep time or arousals — a negative study in a highly symptomatic patient should be escalated to full PSG.
The ESS is subjective and can be under-reported; a normal score does not exclude significant OSA if clinical suspicion is high.
A single night may under-sample events (night-to-night variability); poor sleep or few probe artefacts can invalidate the study.
Consider central sleep apnoea (e.g. heart failure, Cheyne–Stokes) when effort is absent, and other causes of hypersomnolence such as narcolepsy.
🚩 Excessive sleepiness is a driving hazard. Patients with OSA-related sleepiness likely to impair driving must STOP driving and notify the DVLA; driving may resume once symptoms are satisfactorily controlled (e.g. established CPAP). Untreated moderate–severe OSA also carries substantial cardiovascular risk — hypertension, arrhythmia (AF), stroke and myocardial infarction.
🎓 High-yield: ESS > 10–11 flags excessive daytime sleepiness; AHI cut-offs are 5–15 mild, 15–30 moderate, >30 severe. The chest/abdominal effort bands are the discriminator — continued effort against a closed airway = obstructive, absent effort = central.

The Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) is the objective, physiological gold-standard investigation for narcolepsy and other causes of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). It quantifies how quickly a person falls asleep during a series of daytime nap opportunities and whether they enter REM sleep abnormally early. It is always performed the day after an overnight polysomnography (PSG), which both excludes another cause of disrupted nocturnal sleep and confirms the patient had adequate sleep the night before.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to objectively confirm pathological daytime sleepiness and to diagnose narcolepsy, distinguishing it from idiopathic hypersomnia and behavioural sleep deprivation.

In narcolepsy the boundary between wake and REM sleep breaks down (loss of hypothalamic orexin/hypocretin neurons), so the patient falls asleep abnormally fast and jumps straight into REM.
The test measures two variables per nap: sleep latency (time to fall asleep) and the occurrence of a sleep-onset REM period (SOREMP).

Clinical picture prompting the test: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone), sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Preceded by overnight PSG the night before to exclude another cause of sleep disruption (e.g. obstructive sleep apnoea, periodic limb movements) and to document at least ~6 hours of prior sleep.
The patient is offered ~5 scheduled nap opportunities at 2-hourly intervals through the day (typically starting 1.5–3 h after waking).
At each nap the patient lies in a dark, quiet room and is told to try to fall asleep; EEG/EOG/EMG record when sleep onset occurs and whether REM appears.
If no sleep occurs, the nap ends at 20 minutes; if sleep occurs, recording continues ~15 minutes to detect any REM.
🚩 Preparation is critical: REM-suppressing drugs (antidepressants — SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs) and stimulants must be stopped beforehand (usually ≥2 weeks / 5 half-lives), and adequate sleep must be ensured. Screen for shift work and chronic sleep deprivation — these cause false-positive short latencies and spurious SOREMPs.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
Mean sleep latency ≤ 8 minutes→Pathological daytime sleepiness
≥ 2 SOREMPs across the naps (a SOREMP on the preceding night's PSG can count as one)→Supports NARCOLEPSY
Short mean latency BUT no SOREMPs→Idiopathic hypersomnia
Cataplexy + low CSF orexin/hypocretin→Narcolepsy type 1
Narcolepsy confirmed→modafinil (first-line for excessive daytime sleepiness) + sleep hygiene / scheduled naps; cataplexy → an SNRI or sodium oxybate; advise DVLA notification
⏱️Mean sleep latency
≤8 min = pathological sleepiness
🌙SOREMPs
≥2 supports narcolepsy
🧠Narcolepsy type 1
Cataplexy + low CSF orexin
😴Idiopathic hypersomnia
Short latency, no SOREMPs
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Confounders cause false positives: chronic sleep deprivation, shift work and circadian misalignment can shorten latency and trigger SOREMPs, mimicking narcolepsy.
Medications distort results: antidepressants suppress REM (masking SOREMPs, false negative), while abrupt withdrawal of REM-suppressants can cause REM rebound (false positive) — timing of drug cessation matters.
A valid MSLT requires a preceding PSG showing sufficient and undisrupted nocturnal sleep; untreated obstructive sleep apnoea invalidates the interpretation.
🎓 Exam nugget: the classic narcolepsy MSLT result is a mean sleep latency ≤8 min PLUS ≥2 SOREMPs. Remember one SOREMP can be \"borrowed\" from the preceding overnight PSG. Narcolepsy type 1 = cataplexy and low CSF orexin; type 2 lacks both.
SPECIAL TESTS__Hepatology & Biopsy:
The non-invasive liver screen is a standardised panel of blood tests (plus a first-line ultrasound) requested to find the cause of persistently abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) or established chronic liver disease, before or instead of liver biopsy. It systematically screens for the treatable and important aetiologies — viral, autoimmune, metabolic/genetic and lifestyle-related — so that a diagnosis can be reached and disease-modifying treatment started early.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Requested when LFTs are abnormal for more than ~6 weeks (or immediately if decompensated / markedly deranged), or to work up newly-recognised chronic liver disease. The principle is a parallel screen of every common and every dangerous-to-miss cause in one venesection, because clinical features alone cannot distinguish them.

First characterise the pattern of the LFTs, which directs interpretation:

ALT/AST predominant rise→HEPATITIC / hepatocellular picture (viral, autoimmune hepatitis, NAFLD, Wilson's, haemochromatosis)
ALP/GGT predominant rise→CHOLESTATIC picture (PBC, PSC, drugs, obstruction)
Raised GGT with normal ALP→Supports alcohol / enzyme induction rather than bony ALP source
2THE PANEL — BY AETIOLOGY

A killgrid of the standard tests, grouped by the cause each is hunting:

🦠HBsAg
Hepatitis B surface antigen — active HBV infection
🦠HCV antibody
Hepatitis C exposure; confirm activity with HCV RNA
🦠Hep A/E, EBV, CMV
Consider in acute hepatitic pictures
🛡️Immunoglobulins
Raised IgG → autoimmune hepatitis; raised IgM → PBC
🛡️ANA / SMA / anti-LKM1
Autoimmune hepatitis autoantibodies
🛡️AMA
Anti-mitochondrial antibody → primary biliary cholangitis
🩸Ferritin + Tsat
Iron studies for haemochromatosis; confirm with HFE genotyping
🟤Caeruloplasmin
Low in Wilson's disease — especially young patients (± copper studies)
🫁α1-antitrypsin
Low level → α1-antitrypsin deficiency
🍔Glucose / lipids
Metabolic syndrome → NAFLD (commonest cause)
🦋TFTs
Thyroid dysfunction as a driver of abnormal LFTs
🌾Coeliac serology
Anti-tTG — coeliac disease can cause a mild transaminitis
3INTERPRETATION — POSITIVE TEST TO DIAGNOSIS

Map each positive result to the diagnosis it points to:

HBsAg positive→Chronic hepatitis B
HCV antibody + HCV RNA positive→Active hepatitis C infection
Raised IgG + ANA/SMA (or anti-LKM1)→Autoimmune hepatitis
AMA positive + raised IgM + cholestatic LFTs→Primary biliary cholangitis
