Transferrin saturation > 45–50% + raised ferritin→Haemochromatosis → HFE (C282Y) genotyping
Low caeruloplasmin in a young patient→Wilson's disease (confirm with 24h urinary copper, slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings)
Low α1-antitrypsin→α1-antitrypsin deficiency (phenotype/genotype PiZZ)
All serology negative + metabolic risk + bright/fatty liver on US→Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (diagnosis of exclusion)
4IMAGING, PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Ultrasound is first-line imaging alongside the bloods — assesses steatosis, focal lesions, biliary dilatation and signs of cirrhosis/portal hypertension (nodular liver, splenomegaly, ascites).
A normal screen does not exclude significant fibrosis — use non-invasive fibrosis markers (e.g. ELF test, FIB-4, transient elastography) and refer for biopsy if the cause remains unclear or staging is needed.
More than one cause frequently coexists (e.g. NAFLD plus alcohol plus mild iron overload); interpret the whole panel together, not test-by-test.
Caeruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely normal/raised during inflammation, so a normal value does not exclude Wilson's if suspicion is high.
🚩 Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely elevated by inflammation, infection, malignancy or alcohol — do not diagnose haemochromatosis on ferritin alone; interpret with transferrin saturation and confirm with HFE genotyping. And never miss Wilson's disease in a young patient with liver disease — a low caeruloplasmin (with copper studies and slit-lamp examination) is a must-not-miss, as it is treatable and fatal if untreated.
🎓 Learn the antibody triad: anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) → PBC, anti-smooth muscle antibody (SMA)/ANA → autoimmune hepatitis, and remember IgM rises in PBC while IgG rises in autoimmune hepatitis. NAFLD is the commonest cause of mildly abnormal LFTs in the UK but remains a diagnosis of exclusion once the screen is negative.

FibroScan (transient elastography) is a non-invasive, point-of-care ultrasound-based test that measures liver stiffness as a surrogate marker of hepatic fibrosis, greatly reducing the need for liver biopsy. A probe delivers a low-frequency mechanical shear wave into the liver and an ultrasound transducer tracks how fast the wave propagates: the stiffer (more fibrotic) the liver, the faster the wave travels. The result is reported as liver stiffness measurement (LSM) in kilopascals (kPa), with higher values indicating more advanced fibrosis. The same machine reports the Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP) in dB/m, which quantifies hepatic steatosis (fat).

1Indication & principle
Used to stage fibrosis and detect cirrhosis in chronic liver disease without biopsy. The physical principle is shear-wave velocity: a mechanical vibration generates an elastic shear wave, and stiffer tissue conducts it faster (stiffness ∝ velocity²). Because fibrosis and scarring increase tissue stiffness, kPa rises as fibrosis progresses through the METAVIR stages (F0–F4).
MASLD/NAFLD — risk-stratify who needs specialist referral (often combined with FIB-4).
Chronic hepatitis B & C — assess fibrosis and monitor response.
Alcohol-related liver disease — detect advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
Identifying cirrhosis that mandates variceal surveillance and HCC screening.
2How it is performed
Performed at the bedside/clinic in a few minutes. The patient lies supine with the right arm in maximal abduction; the probe is placed in an intercostal space over the right lobe of the liver. The patient should be fasted for at least 2–3 hours (food increases hepatic blood flow and falsely raises stiffness). At least 10 valid measurements are taken and the machine reports the median kPa. Probe size is matched to body habitus (M probe standard; XL probe for higher BMI). Quality/reliability criteria must be met:
≥10 valid readings with a success rate ≥60%.
IQR/median ratio ≤0.30 (a tighter IQR means a more reliable result).
3Interpretation
Higher kPa = more fibrosis. Cut-offs vary by aetiology, but broad bands map onto METAVIR stages. Typical thresholds:
< ~7 kPa→No / minimal fibrosis (F0–F1)
~7–9.5 kPa→Significant fibrosis (F2)
~9.5–12 kPa→Advanced fibrosis (F3)
≥ ~12–15 kPa→Cirrhosis likely (F4) → variceal & HCC surveillance
CAP ≥ ~248 dB/m→Hepatic steatosis present (fat ≥S1)
4Pitfalls & limitations
Several non-fibrotic factors falsely raise stiffness, and body habitus can make readings unreliable. Always interpret in clinical context and check the IQR/success rate.
🔥Acute hepatitis
High ALT / inflammation overestimates stiffness
💧Hepatic congestion
Right heart failure raises kPa spuriously
🟡Cholestasis
Biliary obstruction increases stiffness
🍽️Recent food
Post-prandial hepatic flow → falsely high
⚖️Obesity
Failed/unreliable reading — use XL probe
🌊Ascites
Wave cannot transmit — test unreliable
🚩 Do NOT interpret an elevated stiffness reading in isolation: a raised ALT (acute hepatitis flare), hepatic congestion from right heart failure, or cholestasis can all mimic advanced fibrosis. Ensure the patient is fasted, avoid scanning during an acute hepatitis flare, and only trust a result with an IQR/median ≤0.30 and success rate ≥60%.
🎓 High-yield: think of stiffness ∝ shear-wave velocity² — the faster the wave, the more fibrotic (stiffer) the liver. In MASLD, a low FIB-4 plus liver stiffness <8 kPa reassuringly excludes advanced fibrosis, while ≥12–15 kPa suggests cirrhosis and triggers variceal/HCC surveillance. CAP is the FibroScan parameter for FAT (steatosis), not fibrosis.

Non-invasive liver fibrosis scores are blood-based tools used to risk-stratify patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MASLD) for advanced fibrosis, so clinicians can decide who can be safely reassured in primary care and who needs specialist referral or further testing. They replace routine liver biopsy for most patients, sitting in a stepwise pathway: a simple first-line calculated score (FIB-4) → a second-line serum panel (ELF) or transient elastography (FibroScan) → biopsy reserved for indeterminate or discordant cases.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

NAFLD/MASLD is common, but the prognosis is driven by the degree of fibrosis, not by steatosis or raised transaminases. The aim is to identify the minority with advanced fibrosis (F3–F4) who are at risk of cirrhosis, portal hypertension and hepatocellular carcinoma, while avoiding unnecessary referral of the majority.

FIB-4 combines routine parameters — age, AST, ALT and platelet count — as a cheap, calculable first-line filter available from a standard blood panel.
ELF (Enhanced Liver Fibrosis) is a dedicated serum panel of three matrix-turnover markers reflecting active fibrogenesis, used as a second-line confirmatory test.
NICE recommends testing people with NAFLD for advanced fibrosis using the ELF test, and endorses simple scores such as FIB-4 as an initial step.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Both tests use a single venous blood sample — no fasting, no dynamic protocol.

FIB-4 index = (Age × AST) ÷ (Platelets × √ALT), where age is in years, AST/ALT in U/L and platelets in ×10&sup9;/L. Entered into an online/EPR calculator; no extra assay needed.
ELF measures three markers — hyaluronic acid, procollagen III N-terminal peptide (PIIINP) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1 (TIMP-1) — combined by an algorithm into a single continuous score.
NAFLD Fibrosis Score (NFS) is an alternative simple score using age, BMI, hyperglycaemia/diabetes, AST/ALT ratio, platelets and albumin.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS

FIB-4 gives three bands; ELF is read against a threshold for advanced fibrosis.

FIB-4 < 1.3→LOW risk — advanced fibrosis unlikely; reassure and manage in primary care
FIB-4 1.3 – 3.25→INDETERMINATE — proceed to ELF or FibroScan
FIB-4 > 3.25→HIGH risk — advanced fibrosis likely; refer to hepatology
FIB-4, age > 65 yrs→Use higher low cut-off (~2.0) to reduce false positives
ELF ≥ 10.51→Advanced fibrosis — refer (some services use a local threshold ~9.8)
ELF < 10.51→Advanced fibrosis unlikely — re-test in ~3 years
🧮FIB-4
Age, AST, ALT, platelets — first-line filter
🧪ELF
Hyaluronic acid + PIIINP + TIMP-1 panel
📊NFS
Alternative simple score (adds BMI, diabetes, albumin)
🔊FibroScan
Elastography — second-line after simple score
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
These are risk-stratification tools, not definitive fibrosis staging — a high score prompts referral, it does not confirm cirrhosis.
FIB-4 performs less reliably at extremes of age; it over-calls in the elderly (hence the ~2.0 cut-off >65) and can under-perform in the very young.
Any cause of thrombocytopenia, or an AST rise from a non-hepatic source, can distort FIB-4. ELF can be raised by extrahepatic fibrotic/inflammatory conditions.
Scores validated for NAFLD should not be assumed valid in other liver diseases; the indeterminate band is common and mandates a second test rather than reassurance.
🚩 A low FIB-4 does not exclude significant liver disease — do not use it to override clinical concern such as signs of decompensation, hepatomegaly or jaundice. Extremes of age make FIB-4 unreliable, and a normal ALT never rules out advanced fibrosis in NAFLD.
🎓 High-yield pathway: FIB-4 first → if indeterminate/high, ELF or FibroScan → biopsy only if still unclear. Remember FIB-4 needs Age, AST, ALT, Platelets and its bands 1.3 and 3.25; ELF's three markers are hyaluronic acid, PIIINP and TIMP-1 with the ≥10.51 advanced-fibrosis threshold.

Diagnostic paracentesis (an ascitic tap) is the aspiration of a small volume of ascitic fluid through the abdominal wall for laboratory analysis. It is mandatory in any patient with new-onset ascites, and in any patient with established ascites who is admitted to hospital or clinically deteriorating — its single most important purpose is to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Fluid is also analysed with the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) to separate portal-hypertensive from non-portal causes.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Any patient with new ascites needs a tap to establish the cause, and any cirrhotic with ascites who is admitted, febrile, encephalopathic, has abdominal pain, renal impairment or unexplained deterioration needs a tap to exclude SBP — a spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source. SBP is common (up to ~10–30% of admitted cirrhotics), often asymptomatic, and carries high mortality if missed, so a low threshold to tap saves lives.

Two questions the tap answers: Is it infected? (cell count) and Why is it there? (SAAG).
Physiology: portal hypertension raises hydrostatic pressure and splanchnic vasodilatation, driving a protein-poor, high-gradient transudate into the peritoneum.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED & WHAT TO SEND

Under aseptic technique, a needle is inserted (after ultrasound marking where available) in the left lower quadrant, roughly two-thirds of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine, avoiding scars and the inferior epigastric vessels. Only ~20–30 mL is needed for a diagnostic tap. Send fluid promptly, including inoculating blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield.

Cell count & differential — neutrophil (polymorphonuclear) count is the key SBP test.
Microscopy, Gram stain & culture — ideally in blood-culture bottles.
Protein & albumin — paired with a same-day serum albumin for the SAAG.
Cytology & amylase — when malignancy or pancreatic ascites is suspected; glucose/LDH and AFB/TB culture if indicated.
3INTERPRETATION — SBP & SAAG CUT-OFFS

Two numbers dominate the exam and the ward round: the ascitic neutrophil count (infection) and the SAAG (cause). SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin, both from samples taken the same day.

Ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³→SBP — start empirical antibiotics immediately (do NOT wait for culture)
Neutrophils <250 with a positive culture→Bacterascites — treat if symptomatic; otherwise repeat tap
SAAG ≥11 g/L (HIGH gradient)→Portal hypertension — transudate (cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd-Chiari)
SAAG <11 g/L (LOW gradient)→Non-portal cause — exudate (malignancy, TB, pancreatic, nephrotic)

Management of confirmed SBP: empirical IV cefotaxime or piperacillin-tazobactam, plus IV albumin (classically 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) to reduce hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. After recovery, start secondary antibiotic prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin); consider primary prophylaxis if ascitic protein <15 g/L or after a first SBP.

🩸Cirrhosis
HIGH SAAG ≥11 — commonest cause of portal-hypertensive ascites
❤️Heart failure
HIGH SAAG ≥11 — but ascitic protein is high (>25 g/L)
🫀Budd-Chiari
HIGH SAAG ≥11 — hepatic venous outflow obstruction
🎗️Malignancy
LOW SAAG <11 — peritoneal carcinomatosis; send cytology
🦠TB peritonitis
LOW SAAG <11 — lymphocytic; send AFB & TB culture, ADA
🧪Pancreatic
LOW SAAG <11 — markedly raised ascitic amylase
💧Nephrotic
LOW SAAG <11 — hypoalbuminaemia from urinary protein loss
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
A traumatic (bloody) tap raises the neutrophil count falsely — subtract 1 neutrophil for every 250 red cells/mm³ before applying the ≥250 threshold.
Delay in processing the sample causes cell lysis and an underestimate — send fluid urgently.
SAAG requires same-day serum and ascitic albumin; using mismatched samples invalidates the gradient. SAAG replaces the older, unreliable transudate/exudate protein cut-off.
A moderately deranged clotting/low platelets is not an absolute contraindication to a diagnostic tap; the procedure is low-risk and the diagnostic benefit outweighs bleeding risk.
🚩 An ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ mandates IMMEDIATE empirical antibiotics and IV albumin — never wait for the culture result, and never delay or omit the diagnostic tap in a deteriorating patient with ascites. Missed SBP is rapidly fatal.
🎓 High-yield: SAAG ≥11 g/L = portal hypertension (think “11 or more, pressure at the door”), and a neutrophil count of 250 is the magic number for SBP. Remember to inoculate blood-culture bottles at the bedside to maximise culture yield.

Liver biopsy is the extraction of a small core of hepatic tissue for histological examination. It remains the reference standard for two distinct jobs: grading the necroinflammatory activity of liver disease and staging the degree of fibrosis. It is reserved for when non-invasive tests (FibroScan, ELF, bloods, imaging) are inconclusive, discordant, or when a specific tissue diagnosis is needed (e.g. autoimmune hepatitis, NASH vs simple steatosis, unexplained abnormal LFTs, suspected drug injury, or iron/copper quantification).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why sample the liver

Serum tests reflect liver function/injury but not architecture. Only tissue distinguishes inflammation (grade) from scarring (stage), and only tissue gives a specific diagnosis when the clinical picture is ambiguous.

Diagnosing & staging chronic viral hepatitis (B/C) and autoimmune hepatitis.
Distinguishing NASH (steatohepatitis with ballooning/inflammation) from simple steatosis in NAFLD.
Unexplained persistently abnormal LFTs, suspected drug-induced liver injury.
Quantifying hepatic iron (haemochromatosis) or copper (Wilson disease), and characterising focal lesions.
🎓 Non-invasive tools (transient elastography / FibroScan, ELF blood panel) now diagnose or exclude significant fibrosis in most patients — biopsy is increasingly reserved for the inconclusive or diagnostically difficult case.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — routes & preparation

Pre-procedure: check FBC and clotting, stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets, obtain informed consent, and group & save. The route is chosen by the bleeding risk and presence of ascites.

🧪Percutaneous
Commonest route; ultrasound-guided needle core through the skin. Referred right shoulder-tip pain is typical.
🩸Transjugular
Used with coagulopathy or ascites — bleeding drains into the hepatic vein; also allows portal (wedged) pressure measurement.
🔌Plugged
Percutaneous with the track plugged (gelfoam/coils) as the needle is withdrawn, reducing bleeding in higher-risk patients.

Afterwards the patient lies (often right side) and is observed for several hours to detect bleeding before discharge.

3INTERPRETATION — grading & staging systems

The histopathologist reports two axes: grade (how much active inflammation) and stage (how much fibrosis). Scoring systems standardise this.

METAVIR F0 → F4→Fibrosis stage: F0 none, F1 portal, F2 few septa, F3 many septa, F4 = cirrhosis
Ishak fibrosis 0–6→Finer 7-point fibrosis scale; a separate grade scores necroinflammatory activity
NAFLD Activity Score (NAS)→Sum of Steatosis (0–3) + lobular inflammation (0–3) + ballooning (0–2); ≥5 supports NASH
Stage F4 / Ishak 6→Cirrhosis — triggers surveillance for varices and hepatocellular carcinoma
4LIMITATIONS, CONTRAINDICATIONS & COMPLICATIONS
Sampling error: a core is a tiny fraction (~1/50,000) of the liver — patchy disease (e.g. cirrhosis, PBC) may be under-staged.
Inter-observer variability: different pathologists may assign different grades/stages.
Contraindications: uncorrected coagulopathy (raised INR, low platelets) and tense ascites (favour transjugular route).
🚩 Bleeding is the main and potentially fatal complication. Always check FBC and clotting first — correct coagulopathy or use the transjugular/plugged route. Other risks: pain (referred right shoulder-tip), pneumothorax, bile leak/biliary peritonitis, and rarely death. Observe for several hours post-procedure for haemodynamic instability.
🎓 Grade = inflammatory activity (dynamic, treatable); Stage = fibrosis (structural, slower to change). Examiners love the transjugular indication: coagulopathy or ascites, with the bonus of measuring the hepatic venous pressure gradient.

A renal biopsy is a percutaneous, ultrasound-guided needle sampling of the kidney (usually the lower pole of the kidney) used to diagnose intrinsic renal disease when the diagnosis cannot be made from blood, urine and imaging alone. The cortical core is examined by three complementary techniques — light microscopy (LM), immunofluorescence (IF) and electron microscopy (EM) — and it is the combination of all three that yields the diagnosis. It answers the question 'what is the glomerular/tubulointerstitial process, and can we treat it?'.

1INDICATION — when & why

Biopsy is reserved for cases where the tissue diagnosis will change management. The principle is that many glomerular diseases present with overlapping clinical syndromes (proteinuria, haematuria, falling GFR) but have distinct histology and very different treatments (e.g. immunosuppression vs supportive care).

Nephrotic syndrome in adults — to distinguish minimal change, membranous, FSGS, etc.
Unexplained acute kidney injury — especially suspected rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis or vasculitis.
Nephritic syndrome / glomerulonephritis — haematuria, hypertension, red-cell casts with impaired function.
Unexplained proteinuria or haematuria with renal impairment or rising creatinine of unknown cause.
Renal transplant dysfunction — to diagnose rejection vs calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity vs recurrent disease.
🎓 In a child with classic nephrotic syndrome, biopsy is not first-line: minimal change disease is assumed and steroids given empirically — biopsy only if steroid-resistant or atypical features.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A pre-procedure work-up ensures it is safe, then real-time ultrasound guides a spring-loaded needle to the renal cortex.

Consent and check indication; stop anticoagulants/antiplatelets in advance.
Check clotting (FBC/platelets, PT/APTT) and ensure blood pressure is controlled before proceeding.
Position: patient prone (native kidney) or supine (transplant in iliac fossa); local anaesthetic.
Ultrasound-guided automated needle takes 1–2 cortical cores aiming for the lower pole to avoid the hilar vessels.
Post-procedure: bed rest with observation of pulse, BP and urine for several hours to detect bleeding.

The single core is divided: fixed in formalin for LM, snap-frozen for IF, and placed in glutaraldehyde for EM.

3INTERPRETATION — the three techniques

LM shows overall architecture and patterns; IF shows the pattern of antibody/complement deposition; EM shows ultrastructure and the exact site of deposits. The IF and EM patterns are the classic exam discriminators.

IF: LINEAR IgG along GBM→Anti-GBM disease / Goodpasture
IF: GRANULAR ('lumpy-bumpy') IgG + C3→Immune-complex GN (post-strep, lupus, IgA)
IF: 'FULL HOUSE' (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q)→Lupus nephritis
IF: dominant MESANGIAL IgA→IgA nephropathy (& HSP)
IF: PAUCI-IMMUNE (scanty/no deposits)→ANCA-associated (crescentic) vasculitis / RPGN — urgent immunosuppression ± plasma exchange
EM: foot-process EFFACEMENT, no deposits→Minimal change disease
EM: subepithelial 'HUMPS'→Post-streptococcal GN
EM: subepithelial deposits + 'SPIKES'→Membranous nephropathy
LM: CRESCENTS in Bowman's space→Rapidly progressive GN (urgent)
🔬Light microscopy
Architecture & pattern: sclerosis, crescents, proliferation, thickening.
🟢Immunofluorescence
Deposition pattern of Ig & complement: linear, granular, IgA, pauci-immune.
⚛️Electron microscopy
Ultrastructure: foot processes, humps, spikes, deposit location.
🩸Anti-GBM
Linear IgG on IF; crescents on LM — a medical emergency.
🦋Lupus nephritis
'Full house' IF; subendothelial deposits; wire-loop lesions.
🧬IgA nephropathy
Mesangial IgA on IF; mesangial deposits on EM; commonest GN.
4COMPLICATIONS, CONTRAINDICATIONS & PITFALLS

The kidney is highly vascular, so bleeding is the dominant risk. Careful case selection and correction of clotting/BP beforehand make it safe.

Bleeding / haematuria — the main complication; may form a perinephric haematoma or an arteriovenous fistula.
Pain at the site and infection are less common.
Rarely, uncontrolled bleeding requires embolisation or even nephrectomy.
Contraindications: uncontrolled hypertension, bleeding diathesis/coagulopathy, single functioning kidney (relative), small shrunken (chronically scarred) kidneys, active UTI.
Sampling error: an inadequate core with too few glomeruli can miss focal disease (e.g. FSGS).
🚩 Bleeding is the principal danger. Do NOT biopsy until blood pressure is controlled and any coagulopathy/antiplatelet or anticoagulant effect is corrected — uncontrolled hypertension or a bleeding diathesis can turn a routine biopsy into life-threatening haemorrhage requiring transfusion, embolisation or nephrectomy.
SPECIAL TESTS__Neurology Bedside:
Serial bedside Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) is simple handheld spirometry used to track the strength of the respiratory and bulbar muscles in patients with acute neuromuscular disease — principally Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and myasthenic crisis. It does not diagnose the underlying disease; it is a monitoring test that flags impending neuromuscular respiratory failure so that intubation happens electively rather than as a peri-arrest emergency. The cardinal teaching point is that these patients can tire and decompensate over hours, and by the time blood gases show hypercapnia the patient is already near-terminal.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Any patient with an acute or worsening generalised neuromuscular weakness that could involve the respiratory muscles should have serial FVC. The diaphragm, intercostals and accessory muscles generate the negative pressure that drives inspiration, and the expiratory muscles plus a competent cough clear secretions. As these muscles weaken, the volume the patient can forcibly exhale after a maximal inspiration — the FVC — falls progressively.

GBS: ascending flaccid paralysis; roughly a quarter of patients require ventilation.
Myasthenic crisis: fatiguable weakness worsened by infection, surgery, or drugs, with a fluctuating and sometimes precipitous course.
FVC integrates both inspiratory and expiratory muscle strength and is quick, cheap and repeatable at the bedside.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Use a handheld or bedside spirometer with a tight-fitting mouthpiece (a face mask if bulbar/facial weakness breaks the lip seal). The patient sits upright, takes a maximal breath in, then blows out as hard and completely as possible. Take the best of three attempts and record the absolute value in litres and, ideally, indexed to ideal body weight (mL/kg).

Measure serially, typically every 4–6 hours (more often if falling), and always chart the trend, not just a single number.
A supine FVC that drops markedly compared with sitting suggests diaphragmatic weakness.
A poor lip seal from facial weakness gives a falsely low reading — interpret in context and re-test with a mask.
3INTERPRETATION & THRESHOLDS

Normal FVC is about 60–70 mL/kg. The absolute number, the rate of fall, and the presence of bulbar dysfunction together drive the decision to escalate.

FVC < 20–25 mL/kg→Early warning; increase monitoring frequency, alert ICU/anaesthetics
FVC < 15 mL/kg (or < 1–1.5 L)→Impending respiratory failure — ICU admission and elective intubation
Treat the crisis itself→alongside airway support, give IVIg or plasma exchange — for both GBS and myasthenic crisis. Guillain-Barré syndrome ›
Rapidly falling trend on serial testing→Act on the trajectory even if the current value looks acceptable
Bulbar weakness: weak cough, unsafe swallow, pooling secretions→High aspiration risk; escalate irrespective of the FVC figure
🫁VC < 20 mL/kg
Vital capacity limb of the 20/30/40 rule
💨MIP < 30 cmH₂O
Weak maximal inspiratory pressure (negative)
🌬️MEP < 40 cmH₂O
Weak maximal expiratory pressure — poor cough
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Effort-dependent: fatigue, pain, poor coaching or a broken lip seal all lower the value spuriously.
A single reassuring FVC never excludes deterioration — the value can plummet within hours, especially in myasthenic crisis.
Normal oxygen saturations are falsely reassuring: hypoxia and CO₂ retention are late events, driven by hypoventilation and atelectasis.
Never rely on FVC alone — combine it with clinical signs (rising respiratory rate, staccato/single-breath count speech, orthopnoea, sweating, tachycardia) and bulbar assessment.
🚩 Do NOT wait for hypoxia or a rising PaCO₂ on arterial blood gas — hypercapnia is a LATE, pre-terminal sign of neuromuscular respiratory failure. A rapidly falling FVC, a value approaching 15 mL/kg, or significant bulbar weakness mandates urgent anaesthetic/ICU review for ELECTIVE intubation before the patient decompensates.
🎓 Remember the 20/30/40 rule: VC < 20 mL/kg, MIP (maximal inspiratory pressure) < 30 cmH₂O, or MEP (maximal expiratory pressure) < 40 cmH₂O predicts the need for ventilatory support. The trend and bulbar function matter as much as any single number — a falling FVC with a weak cough is an intubation decision, not an ABG decision.

A DaTscan is a nuclear-medicine SPECT study using the radiotracer ¹²³I-ioflupane (FP-CIT), which binds the presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on the terminals of nigrostriatal neurons in the striatum. Its job is not to name a disease but to answer one binary question: is there a genuine presynaptic dopaminergic deficit? It is most often requested to separate a tremor caused by a neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndrome (reduced uptake) from a tremor with intact dopaminergic terminals such as essential tremor (normal uptake).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

In Parkinson's disease and other degenerative parkinsonian syndromes, the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra degenerate, so their striatal terminals — and the DAT protein they carry — are lost. ¹²³I-ioflupane is a cocaine analogue that binds DAT; the amount of tracer retained in the striatum therefore reflects the density of surviving presynaptic terminals.

Clinical question: is a tremulous or parkinsonian patient's problem due to a presynaptic nigrostriatal deficit, or not?
Classic use: Parkinson's disease vs essential tremor when the diagnosis is clinically uncertain.
Also supports dementia with Lewy bodies (reduced uptake) versus Alzheimer's disease (normal uptake).
2PREPARATION & PROTOCOL
Thyroid blockade: give potassium iodide (or potassium perchlorate) before injection so free radioiodine is not taken up by and does not irradiate the thyroid gland.
Withhold interfering drugs: medications that bind or alter DAT can distort the scan — e.g. cocaine, methylphenidate, amfetamines, some SSRIs and bupropion — and are stopped for an appropriate washout beforehand.
Injection & imaging: ¹²³I-ioflupane is given intravenously; SPECT imaging of the brain is performed after a delay (typically ~3–6 hours) to allow specific striatal binding.
Standard antiparkinsonian dopaminergic drugs (e.g. levodopa) do not significantly affect DAT binding and generally need not be stopped.
3INTERPRETATION — NORMAL vs ABNORMAL

A normal study shows two symmetric comma- or crescent-shaped areas of intense uptake (head of caudate plus putamen) in each striatum. An abnormal study shows reduced and often asymmetric uptake, with the tail of the comma fading so the shape shrinks towards a “full stop” / period — the putamen is affected earliest and most severely.

Symmetric comma/crescent uptake in both striata→NORMAL — intact presynaptic terminals: essential tremor, drug-induced, vascular or psychogenic parkinsonism
Steering treatment→reduced uptake (Parkinson's) → start dopaminergic therapy (levodopa); normal uptake (essential tremor) → first-line propranolol (or primidone). Parkinson's › Essential tremor ›
Reduced / asymmetric uptake shrinking to a “full stop”, putamen first→ABNORMAL — presynaptic dopaminergic deficit: Parkinson's disease, MSA or PSP
Reduced striatal uptake in a patient with cognitive decline→Supports dementia with Lewy bodies over Alzheimer's disease (normal uptake)
🔴Parkinson's disease
Reduced, asymmetric uptake (putamen worst)
🔴MSA / PSP
Also reduced uptake — abnormal like PD
🟢Essential tremor
Normal symmetric uptake
🟢Drug-induced parkinsonism
Normal — terminals intact
🟢Vascular parkinsonism
Normal striatal uptake
🟢Psychogenic tremor
Normal — no presynaptic deficit
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A DaTscan confirms or excludes a presynaptic deficit — it is not a test “for Parkinson's disease” specifically.
Interpretation is partly visual/qualitative, so mild or early cases and poor-quality scans can be equivocal.
Remember interfering drugs and inadequate thyroid blockade as sources of a misleading or technically poor study.
🚩 A DaTscan CANNOT distinguish Parkinson's disease from atypical degenerative parkinsonism (MSA or PSP) — all three show reduced striatal uptake. An abnormal scan means “presynaptic dopaminergic deficit”, and that distinction still rests on the clinical picture, not the scan.
🎓 Think shape: a comma/crescent = normal, a full stop/period = abnormal. The putamen (tail of the comma) is lost first, so early Parkinson's shows an asymmetric “dot” while the caudate head is still preserved.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction, driven by antibodies against the post-synaptic acetylcholine receptor (anti-AChR) or muscle-specific kinase (anti-MuSK). Its hallmark is fatigable weakness — classically ptosis and diplopia that worsen with sustained effort and improve with rest. Two quick bedside tests can support the diagnosis at the ptotic eye: the ice-pack test and the Tensilon (edrophonium) test. Both exploit the same principle — transiently boosting acetylcholine (ACh) availability at the junction — and both should improve ptosis within seconds to minutes.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to support a clinical suspicion of MG in a patient with fatigable ptosis or diplopia, particularly at the bedside or clinic before serology returns. In MG, autoantibodies deplete functional post-synaptic AChRs, so the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission is reduced and weakness fluctuates.

Ice-pack test: cooling reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, so ACh persists longer in the synaptic cleft and transmission transiently improves — the ptotic lid lifts.
Tensilon test: edrophonium is a very short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; blocking ACh breakdown raises cleft ACh and briefly restores transmission.
🧊Ice-pack test
Cold applied to a ptotic lid; safe, no drugs
💉Tensilon test
IV edrophonium; brief dramatic improvement
🧪Anti-AChR
Positive in ~85% of generalised MG
🧬Anti-MuSK
Positive in many AChR-negative cases
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Ice-pack: photograph or measure the resting palpebral fissure / degree of ptosis, apply an ice pack (wrapped in a glove or cloth) to the more ptotic eyelid for about 2 minutes, remove it and immediately re-measure the lid position.
Tensilon: establish IV access with cardiac monitoring and atropine drawn up at the bedside. Give a small test dose of edrophonium (e.g. 2 mg IV), observe for ~30–60 seconds, then give the remaining dose (up to ~8–10 mg total) while watching the target sign (usually ptosis). Effect is transient, lasting only a few minutes.
3INTERPRETATION
Ptosis improves ≥2 mm after ice→Positive ice-pack test — supports MG (high specificity)
Clear, prompt improvement in ptosis after IV edrophonium→Positive Tensilon test — supports MG
No improvement with either test→Negative — does not exclude MG; pursue serology & neurophysiology
Anti-AChR or anti-MuSK antibodies positive→Confirms autoimmune MG (mainstay of diagnosis)
Confirmed MG→symptomatic pyridostigmine + immunosuppression (corticosteroids / steroid-sparing); myasthenic crisis → IVIg or plasma exchange; CT chest for thymoma. Neuromuscular junction disorders ›
Repetitive nerve stimulation shows ≥10% decrement→Supports a neuromuscular transmission defect
Single-fibre EMG shows increased jitter→Most sensitive test for MG — abnormal even when others normal
4PITFALLS, SAFETY & WHAT TO DO NEXT
The ice-pack test is best for ptosis; it is unreliable for isolated ocular motility (diplopia) or limb weakness.
Diagnosis now rests mainly on serology (anti-AChR, anti-MuSK) and neurophysiology — repetitive nerve stimulation (decremental response) and single-fibre EMG (increased jitter, the most sensitive investigation). The Tensilon test is now rarely performed.
Once MG is confirmed, arrange CT of the chest to look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, and screen for associated autoimmune disease (e.g. thyroid).
🚩 Edrophonium can cause dangerous cholinergic side-effects — bradycardia, asystole, hypotension, bronchospasm and excess secretions — and may precipitate a cholinergic crisis. Never give it without cardiac monitoring, IV access, resuscitation facilities and atropine drawn up and ready. Use caution in asthma and cardiac disease.
🎓 The ice-pack test is the high-yield bedside favourite: simple, drug-free, safe and specific. Cold slows acetylcholinesterase, so ACh lingers and the ptotic lid lifts by ≥2 mm after ~2 minutes — a positive result strongly supports myasthenia gravis.

The HINTS exam is a three-part bedside oculomotor battery — Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew — used in acute vestibular syndrome (AVS): rapid-onset, continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus, nausea/vomiting, head-motion intolerance and gait unsteadiness lasting hours to days. Its job is to separate a benign peripheral cause (vestibular neuritis) from a dangerous central cause (posterior circulation / cerebellar stroke). The counter-intuitive core: a pattern that looks “abnormal” on the head impulse is reassuring, while a normal-looking exam is ominous.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — only in continuous AVS with nystagmus

HINTS is validated only in a patient who has ongoing vertigo at the time of examination with spontaneous nystagmus. It is not a test for episodic or positional dizziness (BPPV, that’s Dix-Hallpike) and is meaningless if the patient is symptom-free between attacks.

Principle: an acutely inflamed peripheral vestibular nerve (neuritis) produces a predictable, one-sided, “peripheral” oculomotor signature.
A stroke in the brainstem/cerebellum spares the peripheral vestibulo-ocular reflex, so the head impulse looks deceptively normal while other signs betray central pathology.
In trained hands, HINTS is more sensitive than early MRI-DWI for posterior-circulation stroke in the first 24-48 hours.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the three tests
Head Impulse (head thrust): ask the patient to fixate on your nose; grasp the head and deliver a small, rapid, unpredictable horizontal turn. Watch whether the eyes stay locked on target or need a corrective (refixation) saccade back to it.
Nystagmus: observe the eyes in primary gaze and on lateral gaze to each side. Note the direction of the fast phase and whether it changes with gaze direction, and whether it is horizontal versus vertical/torsional.
Test of Skew (alternate cover test): cover one eye then the other repeatedly while the patient fixates ahead; watch the just-uncovered eye for a vertical corrective movement (skew deviation).
🎓 Do all three at the bedside — no equipment beyond your hands. A single test in isolation is unreliable; interpretation depends on the combined pattern.
3INTERPRETATION — peripheral (reassuring) vs central (INFARCT)
Head impulse ABNORMAL (corrective saccade present)→Peripheral (vestibular neuritis) — reassuring
Head impulse NORMAL (no saccade) despite acute vertigo→Central — worrying for stroke
Nystagmus unidirectional, horizontal, fatigable→Peripheral
Nystagmus direction-CHANGING (gaze-evoked) or vertical/torsional→Central
Test of skew: NO vertical deviation→Peripheral
Test of skew: vertical skew deviation PRESENT→Central

The central pattern is remembered as INFARCT — Impulse Normal, FAst-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test. Any one central feature is enough to mandate stroke work-up.

👋Head Impulse
Abnormal (saccade) = peripheral; Normal = central
👁️Nystagmus
Unidirectional = peripheral; direction-changing/vertical = central
⚖️Test of Skew
No skew = peripheral; vertical skew = central
🚨INFARCT
Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test = stroke
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Wrong context: applying HINTS to episodic or positional dizziness, or to a patient with no spontaneous nystagmus, gives invalid results.
Operator-dependent: sensitivity drops sharply when performed by an untrained examiner — a subtle covert saccade can be missed.
A reassuring peripheral pattern does not override other red flags: sudden severe headache, focal neurology, or inability to stand/walk unaided still warrant imaging.
HINTS-“plus” adds bedside testing of hearing; new unilateral hearing loss with AVS suggests AICA-territory stroke, not neuritis.
🚩 A central / INFARCT pattern — a normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, or skew deviation — or ANY focal neurology or inability to walk unaided, mandates urgent stroke imaging (MRI with DWI) and stroke-pathway referral. HINTS is valid ONLY in continuous acute vestibular syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus; never use it for episodic/positional dizziness.

Audiometric assessment combines quick bedside tuning-fork tests (Rinne & Weber, using a 512 Hz fork) with formal pure tone audiometry (PTA) to detect hearing loss and, crucially, to separate conductive loss (outer/middle ear pathology) from sensorineural loss (cochlea or cochlear nerve). The tuning-fork tests give an instant qualitative answer; PTA quantifies the threshold at each frequency and reveals the diagnostic air–bone gap.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used in any patient with hearing loss, tinnitus, otalgia or aural fullness to triage the type of loss before referral. The principle exploits two sound pathways: air conduction (AC) travels ear canal → tympanic membrane → ossicles → cochlea; bone conduction (BC) bypasses the outer and middle ear, vibrating the skull directly to stimulate the cochlea.

Conductive loss impairs AC but leaves BC intact (the cochlea still works).
Sensorineural loss reduces both AC and BC equally (the cochlea/nerve is the fault).

A 512 Hz fork is standard: low enough to sustain a long tone, high enough not to be felt merely as vibration.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Rinne test (each ear separately): strike the fork, hold the prongs ~1 cm from the ear canal (AC), then place the base on the mastoid process (BC). Ask which is louder / heard longer.

Weber test: strike the fork and place the base on the midline forehead or vertex. Ask where the sound is heard — centrally, or lateralising to one ear.

Pure tone audiometry: performed in a sound-proofed booth. Tones are presented at frequencies 250–8000 Hz via headphones (AC) and a mastoid vibrator (BC). The quietest level heard is the threshold (dB HL), plotted on an audiogram. Tympanometry is added to assess middle-ear compliance (a flat ‘type B’ trace suggests effusion; negative pressure suggests Eustachian dysfunction).

3INTERPRETATION
Rinne POSITIVE: AC > BC→Normal ear OR sensorineural loss
Rinne NEGATIVE: BC > AC→Conductive loss in THAT ear
Weber lateralises TO the poorer ear→Conductive loss on that side
Weber lateralises AWAY (to better ear)→Sensorineural loss on the poorer side
Weber central / midline→Normal or symmetric loss
PTA: air–bone gap ≥ 10 dB→Conductive component present
PTA: AC and BC both reduced, NO gap→Sensorineural loss
Threshold > 25 dB HL (adult)→Abnormal (25–40 mild, 41–70 moderate, 71–95 severe, >95 profound)
4PITFALLS & PATTERNS
False-negative Rinne: in a severe unilateral sensorineural (‘dead’) ear, the mastoid-placed fork is heard by the opposite cochlea via the skull — BC seems > AC, mimicking conductive loss. Masking the other ear resolves it.
Fork frequency matters: a 256 Hz fork is felt as vibration (false results); 1024 Hz decays too fast. Always 512 Hz.
Wax/debris in the canal gives a spurious conductive picture — always otoscope first.

Recognise classic audiogram shapes:

👴Presbycusis
Symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss; age-related, gradual, bilateral.
🔊Noise-induced
Sensorineural notch at 4 kHz with recovery at 8 kHz; occupational/blast exposure.
🦴Otosclerosis
Conductive loss ± Carhart’s notch (dip in BC at 2 kHz); stapes fixation.
🌀Ménière’s
Fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, fullness.
💧Otitis media w/ effusion
Conductive loss + flat (type B) tympanogram; commonest cause in children.
🧠Vestibular schwannoma
Unilateral/asymmetric sensorineural loss ± tinnitus; needs MRI.
🚩 Unilateral or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (or sudden SNHL) must never be dismissed as ‘age’ — it mandates investigation with MRI of the internal acoustic meati to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). Sudden SNHL (over ≤72 hours) is an emergency needing urgent ENT referral and often steroids.
🎓 Memory aid: Rinne tells you which ear’s middle ear is broken; Weber tells you which ear the sound goes to. In pure conductive loss the Weber lateralises TO the affected ear because that ear is shielded from background room noise and hears bone-conducted sound better — the counter-intuitive point examiners love.
